title: Land rights shake-up for remote Top End, with creation of new council
text:
A powerful Yolŋu leader has announced the creation of a breakaway remote Northern Territory land council to help drive direct economic development for his people.

Gumatj Corporation leader Djawa Yunupiŋu used his keynote Garma Festival speech in north-east Arnhem Land to announce the shake-up to the NT's current land rights system.

"We are going to the top of the mountain," Mr Yunupiŋu said.

The creation of the Dilak Land Council would put the ability to make economic development decisions into the hands of his people, and away from the powerful Northern Land Council (NLC) which oversees communities across much of the Top End.

"It will be the power for our future," he said.

"The Northern Land Council was a vision of our elders, who knew that one day, when the time was right, the power would be brought back fully into the hands of land owners, as it should be."

Gumatj Corporation leader Djawa Yunupiŋu has announced the formation of the new Dilak Land Council during a Garma Festival keynote address. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

'New life to the land and the people'

The announcement coincides with the 50th anniversary of the creation of the federal Aboriginal Land Rights Act, passed by Malcolm Fraser's government in 1966.

Mr Yunupiŋu announced the new land council in front of high-profile delegates including Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Timor Leste Prime Minister Xanana Gusmão.

The NLC has been criticised in recent years for its perceived delays in granting land tenure permits for those wanting to set up businesses on Aboriginal land in the Top End.

It also controls the distribution of mining royalties across territory communities.

Mr Yunupiŋu said it was his hope that the Dilak Land Council, which would represent the 13 clan groups of the Gove Peninsula, would give his people the ability to liaise directly with those wanting to do business on Yolŋu land.

"The Dilak council will give new life to the land and the people," he said.

"It will work with the government, and mining companies, and any company who wants to do business with us.

"We will work in partnership with the Northern Land Council, for the people.

"We will be a part of the economic life of this nation, while never losing who we are, and what we stand for."

The Dilak Land Council would put the ability to make economic development decisions into the hands of his people, and away from the powerful Northern Land Council, says Mr Yunupiŋu. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

Arnhem region's uncertain future

In recent years, Mr Yunupiŋu's Gumatj Corporation has been at the forefront of business development in north-east Arnhem Land.

Garma promise on land rights anniversary NT leader Lia Finocchiaro uses her first Garma Festival speech to promise land and fuel security in north-east Arnhem Land after its main employer, Rio Tinto, leaves town.

The company built and runs its own timber mill and furniture business, facilitates rocket launches on a remote launch site, and recently took over a shopping centre complex.

It comes as the north-east Arnhem region faces an uncertain future, with the impending closure of its main employer, a Rio Tinto bauxite mine, in 2029.

Mr Yunupiŋu has long been an executive member sitting on the NLC board, though it is currently unclear whether he still holds that role.

The NLC has been approached for comment.

title: Boxer earns Tuvalu's first ever Comm Games medal without winning fight
text:
A boxer from Tuvalu earned her tiny South Pacific nation's first ever Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight overnight.

Tarona Taafaki lost her only bout in the women's 75-kilogram class to India's Lovlina Borgohain, losing every round on all three of the judges' cards.

Because there were only five entrants, Taafaki received a bye to the last four, meaning she was automatically guaranteed at least a bronze medal.

Tarona Taafaki arrives at the Commonwealth Games during the opening ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

But her coach and father said the population of Tuvalu, an island south-east of Tonga, will celebrate the medal and use it to highlight a climate change emergency.

Badi Taafaki, whose son Pasoni competed earlier in the Games and lost his only bout at 70kg, told the British Press Association: "For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything.

"We're one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it's a stepping stone."

Tarona and Pasoni are the two eldest of eight children, all of whom are boxers. They are based in New Zealand in order to take advantage of better facilities.

"My children are very fortunate," Badi said.

"They have opportunities and facilities that I never had. Boxing is our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline."

Athletes on the island famously train on its airport runway, the most stable land mass on an island increasingly threatened by rising sea levels. Climate experts predict half of the nation's capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050.

A group of locals play volleyball on the airport runway in Funafuti, Tuvalu. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

"Yes, we train on the airport runway," Badi said. "When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.

"If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change.

"It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades. Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can't sleep if there's a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes."

Tarona is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia's Taylah Robertson picked up a bronze in the women's flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her bout to England's Lisa Whiteside.

title: Six new bird flu cases suspected in Victoria
text:
Six more suspected cases of H5N1 bird flu have been detected in the state's south-west.

The Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) said preliminary testing had identified five crested terns suspected to have the deadly disease.

Three of the birds were located in Portland, and two in nearby Nelson Bay.

Some of the suspected cases have been identified in Portland, in Victoria's south-west. (ABC News: Emily Bissland)

The samples will undergo further testing at the CSIRO's Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness.

A further suspected case was announced yesterday in Portland.

Victoria's first positive case of H5 bird flu was confirmed on Thursday, also in Portland.

Local transmission in Australia

Earlier this week, local transmission of H5 bird flu occurred for the first time between a number of greater crested terns in South Australia.

The H5N1 strain was first detected in Australia in a brown skua discovered in the Cape Le Grand National Park near Esperance, about 700 kilometres south-east of Perth, in June, and has since spread across the southern coast through migratory bird populations.

There have since been additional cases in WA, SA, New South Wales, and Queensland.

Community assistance vital

Victorian Chief Veterinary Officer Graeme Cooke said community observations are important to help authorities monitor and detect the disease.

Graeme Cooke says community observations help authorities monitor for H5N1. (ABC News)

"Their reports support ongoing surveillance and help ensure samples can be collected and tested as quickly as possible," he said.

" Our teams are out in the field every day, conducting surveillance, collecting samples and working with local communities and landholders to monitor the situation and support response activities. "

He urged Victorians to avoid contact with sick or dead wildlife and to record and report what they see.

"Early reporting remains one of the most important tools we have for monitoring the spread of the disease," Dr Cooke said.

title: One young Aussie hopes to silence Glasgow on the last night at Scotstoun
text:
The mile world record had been stuck at four minutes, 1.4 seconds for nine years when England's Roger Bannister stepped onto the track at Oxford in May, 1954.

Near the same university where he earned his medical degree, Bannister operated with surgical precision to reach his ultimate goal of becoming the first man to dip under four minutes for the mile.

But, as is so often the case, once a barrier is broken, it reminds others they too can do what just yesterday seemed impossible.

And, sure enough, 45 days later Australian John Landy went around the Turku track in Finland four times in 3:58 flat.

It set the stage for the so-called Miracle Mile at the 1954 British Empire and Commonwealth Games.

Roger Bannister (329) in action against John Landy. (Getty Images: Mark Kauffman/Sports Illustrated)

It was a moment when the sporting world's eyes were firmly locked on Vancouver, regardless of any connection to the Commonwealth, to watch the best middle distance runners to that point in history face off.

Eight runners made it to the final, but all eyes were on just two as Bannister, who set his sub-four-minute mark of 3:59.8 on a home track with friends pacing for him, would face Landy in the purest competition settings.

The Australian took the lead after one lap and led for the next kilometre and change, going out hard in an attempt to use his superior stamina, as Bannister called it, to negate the Englishman's famous final burst.

Roger Bannister breaks the tape in the one-mile final in Vancouver. (Getty Images)

Having felt Bannister on his heels and seen his shadow sticking firm under him for the entire race, Landy took one look over his left shoulder about 100 metres out on the final bend, and in that moment Bannister burst past unsighted on the right and flew home to victory.

Both runners finished under four minutes, marking another piece of history.

An exhausted Bannister after the race. (Getty Images: Fox Photos)

A 60-year sabbatical

Despite that glorious event, and a race of almost exactly 1,600 metres seeming to make sense on the world-standard 400m track, the mile was only run at three more Commonwealth Games before swapping it out for the 1,500m after 1966.

New Australian record holder Cameron Myers said it can become prestigious once again.

"I think it's a way we can attract more people into the sport," he said.

"Americans still love it, so I think it's just something that regular people can resonate a little bit more with."

Cameron Myers is supremely confident in his mile. (AP: Alastair Grant)

At the time of its last Commonwealth outing in Kingston, the Caribbean nations were yet to become the sprint powerhouses we now know them to be, so the mile had been considered the blue-riband event at the Games.

And it returns 60 years later, with Glasgow hoping to host another historic night tonight.

"It's obviously a very prestigious part of the Commonwealth Games and its history, so it's really exciting that it's come back in this year and allowed us to attack it," said Abbey Caldwell, one of three Australian competitors in the women's final.

Abbey Caldwell is part of Australia's stacked middle-distance stocks. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Caldwell will run alongside Jessica Hull and Claudia Hollingsworth from 6:45am (AEST), and she believes they have a genuine chance of a podium sweep.

"There's always the pressure of you want to go and achieve those medals, and you want to be the first Australians to do that," she said.

"But we're also in a very fortunate position to have three very strong Australians going into this, so it's a really nice opportunity for us to go take those history books and cement them as Australians."

Jess Hull (second from right) leads an elite pack of Australian middle distance runners. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Whether they win them or not, the men (from 5:55am) will get the honour of running for the first Commonwealth Games mile medals in six decades.

And in that race lies a chance for Australia to reverse the misery of Bannister's late pass in 1954.

Young Aussie wants to spoil the party

Including Bannister's first trip under the milestone mark, the mile record was broken 19 times in 44 years, when the great Moroccan Hicham El Guerrouj ran 3:43.13 in 1999.

His record stood for 27 years, which the astute among you may recognise as bringing us up to the here and now.

Well, two weeks ago, to be exact.

Josh Kerr played up to the crowd as he qualified for the final. (Supplied)

Just before the start of the Glasgow Games, Scottish 1,500m world champion Josh Kerr ran 3:42.66.

Just two weeks earlier at prestigious Prefontaine Classic, 20-year-old Myers broke Ollie Hoare's Australian record, running 3:46.06, setting up a tantalising shootout on the mile's return.

"Kerr's going to want to make a move at some point, and he's shown he's the fittest in the field," Myers said.

"I think he'll want to make a move and I'm not going to let him go."

Landy described the Miracle Mile as "like a title fight", and just like a battle for a belt, styles make fights.

We saw a preview in their separate heats, where both won but Myers was five seconds faster than Kerr.

Myers jumped to the front of his pack and led the whole way home with clinical efficiency, while Kerr sat in the pack until the last lap before ambling to the front and revving up the crowd with 150 metres to go.

Josh Kerr fired up the Glasgow crowd as he coasted into the final. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The Scotstoun Stadium crowd will be baying for Kerr and 2022 world champion in the 1,500m Jake Wightman, but young buck Myers is out to prove himself in an elite field.

"I'm a competitor, I don't want to lose," he said.

"I'm not going there to come second, so I'll have a crack at him the best I can and if I blow up trying, so be it.

"Everyone's cheering for the Scots, and I'm sure they want to go 1-2, so I'm trying to spoil that."

The mile start line sits 9.34 metres behind the start/finish line. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Myers will also be running alongside teammates, with reigning 1,500m Commonwealth champion Ollie Hoare and 24-year-old Adam Spencer making it through.

The final night of the athletics program on the penultimate day of the Games feels like the perfect time for a clash between the hosts and the runaway medal tally toppers.

If the Aussies can ruin the party, they would have done what Landy couldn't 72 years ago.

And Myers is well aware of the opportunity in front of him.

"Hopefully I can reverse the roles."

title: Deep connections drive burial growth in historic WA town
text:
Shire of York president Chris Gibbs only moved to the historic town in recent years, but has already decided he wants to be buried there.

"I have no intention of leaving York, this is where I've decided to make a life," he said.

York, which is 100 kilometres east of Perth in Western Australia, has the claim of the country's oldest inland town.

Chris Gibbs says people continue to be buried in York after forming a strong connection to the town. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Mr Gibbs said many people within the town and others who were moving back to York had a strong emotional connection to the place.

"If I was to spend the rest of my days here, why wouldn't I personally want to be laid to rest in a town I helped contribute to and felt like I belonged to?" he said.

"It doesn't have to be someone with a long history in a town who chooses to be buried here.

"It can be someone who starts their family's story in this town by choosing to be laid to rest in a place they loved and they have connection to.

"I can only see that increasing as people continue to move to York."

The Shire of York says the local cemetery is reaching capacity. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Shire of York chief executive Alina Behan said a combination of an aging population and community connection had led to the need for another cemetery.

"People book [burials] 25 years ahead to make sure they can actually get their plot of land here at York so they can continue, whether it's a family tradition or just keep that association to the place they have lived in and loved," she said.

"It obviously is a popular place to be buried."

Oldest inland town

Despite having three cemeteries, the shire is looking at creating a new burial site as the current one will soon reach capacity.

Historians estimate there are 600 people buried in the historical portion of the York Cemetery, which was established in 1874.

In addition, more than 400 potential unmarked graves were identified after archaeological surveying works in 2023, with initial research into historical records indicating multiple burials in the same grave site.

Hundreds more are buried throughout the modern blocks.

The York Cemetery at Mount Brown was allocated in 1874. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

With more than half of the town's residents aged over 55, York has the oldest median age in the state, sitting at 56 years of age, leading the local government to plan for future burial demand.

Mr Gibbs said the longevity of regional cemeteries was vital to the preservation and continuation of history.

"Regional cemeteries paint a history of the region and the town, and as the towns continues on and we continue to lay our loved ones to rest it creates a map of where we have come from and where we're going," he said.

"As a society we all need a place where we can look back at where we came from."

Metro cemeteries out of space

As a way to combat space limitation, Perth's Karrakatta Cemetery has a renewal program that involves land between burial plots being used to create more gravesites, relocating already existing headstones.

More than 9,000 new gravesites and 30,000 memorial locations have been created since the program began in the mid-1990s.

Grants of burial are given a tenure of 25 years before renewal works are considered, with possible time-frame extensions.

Karrakatta Cemetery's renewal program involves land between burial plots being used to create more gravesites. (ABC News: Emma Wynne)

Mr Gibbs said he did not want to see York replicate Karrakatta's solution out of respect for those who had passed.

"Could you do this is a very different way that required a lot less land? Absolutely," he said.

"But life needs to be treated with respect.

"I wouldn't want to see cemeteries based only on practicalities and efficiency.

"I think we need to hold firm on that."

Burials into the future

Elaine Huddy's daughter Tabatha was buried at the York Cemetery in 1979, passing at just one hour old after being diagnosed with spina bifida at birth.

She was not able to hold her daughter and does not have a photograph of her, but one day hopes to be buried alongside her at the York Cemetery.

Elaine Huddy wants to be buried with her daughter Tabatha in the town she considered her home. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

Ms Huddy, 68, has lived in York on and off for the past 58 years, spending time in Perth and Indonesia between returns to her home town.

She said despite her travels, she had remained connected to the town through the strong sense of community.

"Even though I have come and gone, this is home. It has always been home," Ms Huddy said.

Ms Huddy said having a cemetery in York meant she was able to celebrate her daughter and visit her regularly as part of her grieving process.

Tabatha Wheeler was laid to rest in York Cemetery. (ABC Midwest and Wheatbelt: Eliza Bidstrup)

"When it was Tabatha's 40th birthday, myself, her father and our two children and grandchildren came up to the cemetery to celebrate," she said.

"Having her close to home means she is never far away."

The Shire of York says modelling indicates a new site will be needed in the next five years but could be available as soon as next year pending identification and testing of the grounds.

title: WA set to fall short of vaccination target as free flu jabs come to an end
text:
Western Australia is set to fall short of the ambitious vaccination targets it set ahead of the flu season.

After the state experienced its worst season since at least 2001 last year, which was blamed in part on poor vaccination rates, the government set what it described as "ambitious" targets.

But the government's extended free flu vaccination program ended yesterday, with immunisation rates still a way off from the targets.

The targets included protecting 30 per cent of babies and young children under 12 years, lifting coverage to 65 per cent for people aged 65 and over, and setting a new "benchmark immunisation rate" across the state of 40 per cent of the population vaccinated.

WA records worst-ever flu season amid poor vaccination rates Western Australia records its worst flu season on record, with more than 30,000 influenza cases reported this year.

But according to the most recent data, issued on Monday, the state was still well short of its ambitions.

Senior West Australians came closest to their target, just over 6 per cent off the 65 per cent target.

Children between six months and 12 years old were next closest, falling 6.5 per cent short of their aim.

The gap was nearly double for the general population though, with just 28 per cent of West Australians getting jabbed, well short of the 40 per cent target.

Free vaccinations a 'good job'

Vaccination policy researcher Katie Attwell said the government was in a difficult position because hitting the targets was always going to be challenging.

"There can be so many reasons that doesn't occur, but that doesn't mean that governments [shouldn't] stick their neck out and say, 'Yeah, we really want this, we are really putting a whole of government approach behind this,'" the University of Western Australia professor said.

Katie Attwell says vaccine goals can be difficult. (ABC News: Herlyn Kaur)

"Because that also sends an important signal, but importantly, also, it unlocks the machinery of government to make sure that they are doing everything they can be doing to make it easy enough for us to go and do what they would like us to do."

Professor Attwell said the government had done a "really good job" at trying to increase vaccination rates, including making it free.

That work was part of a more than $100 million plan to help the health system prepare for flu season, including by paying for beds in private hospitals.

More accessible vaccinations

In a statement, a WA government spokesperson said flu and RSV vaccinations had been made "more accessible than ever before".

"We've introduced the needle-free FluMist option for children, facilitated pop-up vaccination clinics and increased pharmacy vaccination access.

FluMist is a nasal vaccine designed for children who are anxious about needles. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"As of 26 July, more than 860,000 Western Australians have received an influenza vaccination.

"Influenza notifications and hospitalisations for the year to date are lower compared to the previous five-year average."

The spokesperson added, however, that RSV notifications and hospitalisations were higher.

"This serves as a strong reminder to parents of infants, pregnant women and people over the age of 75 to get their free RSV vaccination.

"Over 100,000 Western Australians have accessed their free RSV vaccination this year, in comparison to 20,156 Western Australians in 2025."

Do you know more? Contact Keane Bourke on encrypted email. Please note you will need your own encrypted email account, such as Protonmail, to ensure end-to-end encryption.

Opposition health spokesperson Libby Mettam said she was not surprised the government had fallen short of its targets.

"We had called for the Cook Labor government to introduce the flu vaccination earlier, which would have given people more options and ensured that it was also more accessible," she said.

Flu cases drop

This year's flu season appears less serious than last year's, with about 5,340 cases reported to WA Health between January and June, about a third of the 16,495 infections reported over the same period last year.

RSV infections, on the other hand, are up compared to 2025, with 6,658 cases reported to authorities so far this year, compared to 6,242 last year.

This is why the government is still encouraging people to take advantage of free RSV vaccines, which are available for some pregnant women, infants, children and older West Australians.

Ambulance ramping, one of the clearest signs of how much pressure hospitals are under, was higher than last month, with ambulances spending 5,924 hours parked outside of hospitals waiting to transfer patients.

But that is lower than both July 2024 and 2025.

Libby Mettam says ambulance ramping has hit "horror" levels. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

"We have become accustomed to record levels, and horror levels, of ambulance ramping in our hospital system," Ms Mettam said.

"Over 5,600 hours represents a horror story for many patients, but also our healthcare workers who continue to do more with less."

Ms Mettam said it was down to luck that flu rates were lower, and the health system was able to cope better, rather than the government's efforts.

An increasing challenge

Improving vaccination rates has been an increasing challenge for health authorities in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

80,000 kids aged five and under behind on vaccinations The latest immunisation data shows more than 80,000 Australian children aged five and under are not fully up to date with their vaccinations.

Professor Attwell said there were no simple solutions, but it was important for governments and researchers to continue trying to understand why people are not getting vaccinated.

"It's easy to draw the wrong conclusions about why vaccination isn't occurring," she said, urging people not to write off those who are not immunised.

Instead, Professor Attwell said it was important to ask questions like: "How do we reach those people? What is standing in their way? What worries do they have?

"There will be segmentation of that population with different reasons underpinning why this year, so far, this hasn't been the offer that they're ready to take up," she added.

But she remained optimistic that if the government kept showing up and trying to reach more people, its efforts would be successful in the long run.

Katie Attwell says continued efforts to vaccinate more people would be successful in the long term. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

AMA WA president Kyle Hoath said it was up to everyone to improve vaccination rates.

"Immunisation is one of the most effective and cost-efficient public health measures we have, and it saves lives," he said.

"Higher vaccination rates help to protect the Western Australian population, particularly in the winter months when the flu is prevalent.

"We encourage all Western Australians to have their flu shot, protecting themselves, and doing their bit to protect fellow Western Australians."

title: Pet dogs trained to sniff out black truffle treasure worth $2,000 per kg
text:
A ragtag group of farm dogs and pets of different breeds and sizes are assembled in a paddock just outside Narooma on the New South Wales South Coast.

Their owners are nervous but excited about the prospect of testing their dogs' sniffing skills in a training class to see if they have what it takes to hunt for truffles.

Self-taught truffle hunter Kate Le Bars runs the classes, having spent the past seven years professionally locating the luxury fungus with her nine-year-old Australian Koolie, Hepburn.

"It's magical working with your dog and coming out to find the buried treasure," she said.

"On a beautiful day, it doesn't feel like work; it is just fun."

Kate Le Bars and her dog Hepburn work at the truffiere. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

With black truffles priced at about $2,000 per kilogram, turning the real thing into a training tool would be an expensive exercise, so a cotton ball dipped in a pungent synthetic truffle scent is used instead.

The lesson is simple enough: owners say the word truffle, then show their dog the cotton ball.

If the dog can then locate the cotton ball when the owner next says the magic word, they get a treat.

Ms Le Bars said as long as the dog had the right training, focus and responsiveness to rewards, any breed could pick up the skill.

"We had a Lagotto in one class, who were bred specifically to find truffles … and actually [a] little hairy white dog was the star," she said.

A mix of working dogs and lap dogs attend a truffle training class in Narooma. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Truffle boom

Since their introduction to local soils less than 30 years ago, Australia has fast become the world's fourth-largest truffle producer.

Truffle hunting was traditionally performed by pigs, but as they would often eat the treasure after finding it, dogs and their 300 million olfactory receptors have emerged as more cost-effective sniffers.

Australian Koolie Hepburn can find up to 60 truffles in an hour of sniffing. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

If a dog does well in class, they are invited to the Gulaga Gold truffiere at Dignams Creek, south of Narooma.

"It usually takes one truffle season for them to be able to get to a stage where they're good enough, and then the next truffle season they become a professional truffle hunter," Gulaga Gold owner Fiona Kotvojs said.

Fiona Kotvojs owns the only commercial trufferie on the NSW South Coast. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

A successful truffle hunter will avoid distraction and sniff out the odour plume or "cone" that comes off the mycorrhizal fungus.

When they find the source, they place a delicate paw to indicate the location and not disturb the underground delicacy.

Black truffles can retail for about $2,000 per kilo. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Up to 60 truffles can be sniffed out under the oak and hazelnut trees in an hour and marked with flags to be dug out later.

Australia is the fourth-largest producer of truffles globally, with commercial truffieres across the country. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

Sniffing success

The class has a mixed success rate, with only the cream of the crop making it out to the truffiere.

Some class attendees are there to learn skills for their own businesses, like Olivier Kapetanakos from Jindabyne, who has his own 2-hectare truffiere that is ready for its inaugural winter harvest.

He brought along his three-year-old cocker spaniel Ted, an energetic "failed medic dog", for his first day of truffle training.

Ted flunked out of being a medic dog, but his owners hope he will have more success finding truffles. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

"He's motivated by food, he's motivated by being with us," Mr Kapetanakos said.

"It's now just about channelling that enthusiasm to finding the truffle."

For others, the class is a fun way to test the teamwork between dog and owner, with the building blocks of the scent training able to be applied to anything.

"We had one person that was very keen to teach the dog to sniff out her wallet or her keys when she lost them," Ms Le Bars said.

"It's really good for the dogs. They love doing it.

" Anything the dog loves doing is worth encouraging in my experience. "

Kate Le Bars says teamwork between owner and dog is key. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

title: 'A miracle': World's largest gold bar made in Australia
text:
A gold bar produced in Western Australia weighing more than half a tonne has claimed the Guinness World Records title for the world's largest gold bar.

The Perth Mint created the 521.2 kilogram bar using Australian gold, refined to a 99.999 per cent purity.

Mint chief executive Paul Graham said the current world standard was 99.99 per cent.

"To get to five-nines gold, 99.999, not many can do that," he said.

More than 35 specialists were involved in the project. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

" It's nothing short of a miracle. "

The achievement broke the previous world record of 300 kilograms, set by a mint in Dubai two years ago.

What's the point?

A team of more than 35 specialists were involved in the project, which Mr Graham labelled the "People's Bar".

Mr Graham said the idea for the project came a year ago, with the Mint conducting a "practice run" ahead of the bar's creation.

He said officials from the Guinness Book of World Records attended on site to watch every step of the process, which took up to three days.

Paul Graham says it's a "miracle" to produce such a big gold bar at 99.999 per cent purity. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

As for what the record-breaking bar was worth, Mr Graham said he wished he knew.

"Naturally most people work out that the metal price alone is over $100 million, but something that unique, it's never been done before," he said.

As to the purpose, the bar serves as promotion of the Perth mint and its capabilities.

The Mint said the spectacle would help showcase the expertise of its local refiners and Australia's gold industry to the world.

It will eventually be on display at the Mint alongside another record-breaking creation, a one tonne gold coin unveiled in 2011.

Gold exports grow

Australia's gold export earnings are forecast to grow to $60 billion in 2025-26 from $47 billion in 2024-25, according to the Minerals Council of Australia (MCA).

Mr Graham says the gold bar's metal price is over $100 million. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

That trajectory would see gold become Australia's second-largest export earner after iron ore, the MCA said.

The price of spot gold was about $US4,079 per ounce on Friday, according to the global financial data provider LSEG.

title: Nina Kennedy is often superhuman, but in Glasgow she was a super human
text:
That's not how this was meant to go.

When Nina Kennedy steps into an athletics arena, the expectation is gold, and she carries herself accordingly.

The definition of a smiling assassin, Kennedy's friendly demeanour disguises a competitor's heart that beats with propulsive force.

It launches her down the runway and, usually, to great heights.

In Glasgow, Kennedy fell short of her own lofty goals and the standards we've come to expect from her, but still came away with silver in the women's pole vault final, albeit in a final that won't go down as one of the greats.

Kennedy snags silver, teen grabs surprise gold Flag bearer Nina Kennedy settles for silver in the pole vault and Australia's sprint stars return to the track after a host of medals at the velodrome.

Tailwinds at Scotstoun Stadium have been helping the sprinters, hindering the throwers, terrifying the hurdlers, and on Friday night, local time, making life difficult for the vaulters.

The crosswind kept the final from being a true jump-off between the strong field, with Kennedy clearing the bar only three times from seven attempts and 2016 Olympic bronze medallist Eliza McCartney winning on countback.

The top clearance of 4.65 metres by the gold and silver medallists was 30 centimetres lower than both of their personal bests.

Nina Kennedy came to Glasgow for gold. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Kennedy topped by 1-centimetre McCartney's eight-year-old Oceania record of 4.94m just a couple of weeks before the Commonwealth Games began.

So, despite sporting a pretty gnarly scar from last year's hamstring surgery, there's no question Kennedy was fit and in form.

She carried her typical energy into the final, sitting out the early heights and waiting in the tall grass for her chance to pounce once half her competitors had already X'd out.

Why no other runner embraced the 200m gold medallist A doping scandal dating back to 2024 was the backdrop of the women's 200m final in Glasgow, and the frosty post-race scenes.

By the time she got out of her thick coat and stood at the top of the runway, piercing blue eyes fixed on her first attempt at 4.45m, half the eight-woman field was already gone.

She got over on her first go, but not with the sort of convincing clearance over the bar we were used to seeing.

Conserving energy? Shaking off the cold? No, as it turned out. Just a tricky competition.

New Zealander Olivia McTaggart stumbled at that hurdle three times, assuring Kennedy of a medal — and most likely silver at least after 2022 bronze medallist Imogen Ayris took three tries to clear 4.30m — but minor medals are not what Kennedy came here for.

Kennedy cleared 4.65m as her top vault. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The 29-year-old has been in Glasgow as long as any of Australia's 255-strong team, having arrived early to carry the flag in the opening ceremony.

She has been so ever-present around the team that her success feels even more inevitable than usual, especially for folks who may have only watched her jump at Commonwealth Games, worlds and Olympics.

In those competitions, she had gone gold, gold, gold since her breakthrough win in Birmingham.

But so many things have to go right for an athlete to consistently catapult themselves 5 metres into the air with the accuracy and control required, and sometimes the pieces just don't quite fit.

Pole vault is hard enough in perfect conditions. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

By the time she was preparing for her third attempt at 4.70m, the stare no longer looked so steely.

Having missed three of her last four jumps to that point, it didn't feel like a foregone conclusion that she'd pull it out in the clutch yet again, and so it proved.

"Of course I'm disappointed, I wanted to win, and I didn't," she said, emphasising that she was "genuinely really happy" to see veteran McCartney win her first major international gold.

"I'm superhuman most of the time, but I'm also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes, and that's OK.

"I'm a high achiever, and I push myself to be that, but I think it's also important to remember I'm human and I make mistakes. I didn't want to make mistakes out there tonight, but I did, and that's OK."

The epitome of a big-moment performer, Kennedy has now not been able to defend her 2023 world or 2022 Commonwealth Games titles.

She missed the 2025 athletics world championships because of her torn hamstring and missed the mark in Glasgow, but results aren't all that matter for a woman who has ticked off every career goal at this point.

Kennedy was thrilled for Eliza McCartney (centre) to get her first major international gold medal. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

She said before the opening ceremony that she would probably forget to soak in the moment as the team's flag-bearer, but after a long campaign and a surprisingly short time on centre stage, it seems she has figured it out.

"Sometimes sport is more than just the medals, it's about the memories made and the connections and the officials and the volunteers," she said.

"The crowd out there was so awesome. Everyone was just so happy to be here. I'm walking away with a lot of memories.

"I'm happy. Like, I'm sad, but I'm happy."

title: FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plans after global backlash
text:
World football's governing body, FIFA, says it has scrapped plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors after widespread backlash.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said in a statement: "Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place."

Senior FIFA advisor quits post A senior advisor to FIFA President Gianni Infantino resigned in protest at plans to sell a stake in the World Cup.

The plan was to raise $US4.2 billion ($5.9 billion) by selling about a 20 per cent stake in a new unit that would run FIFA events, including the World Cup, valuing it at $US20 billion.

The proposal, first announced on Tuesday, was strongly opposed by European football's governing body, UEFA, which threatened a boycott and accused FIFA of putting the sport's "soul" up for sale.

Mr Infantino said in his statement: "[The] FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed.

"Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve."

FIFA had argued that selling the minority stake in its commercial operations would raise billions of dollars to fund global sports development, and accused the media of mischaracterising the proposal.

Mr Infantino had written to member associations to tell them they would receive $US40 million each if they agreed to FIFA's proposal by September 19.

Gianni Infantino's proposal received pushback from all corners of the football world. (AP: Eduardo Verdugo, File)

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support," Mr Infantino said in Friday's statement.

Opposition to the plan snowballed over the week

On Thursday, UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments until the proposal was withdrawn, saying that the World Cup "cannot be treated as an investment product".

The 41-member federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean (CONCACAF) rejected the proposal during a meeting on Thursday.

On Friday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which has 47 members, issued a statement saying it "stands in solidarity" with UEFA and CONCACAF.

UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC combined have 143 national associations, well over half of FIFA's 211 members. A majority of the members would have needed to vote in support of the plan for it to proceed.

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

Disagreement was also internal.

On Friday, Mr Infantino's senior adviser, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned with immediate effect, calling the plan "a bad deal for football", while FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been "deceived" by Mr Infantino, describing the proposal as a "project of one person".

Mr Infantino, 56, is up for re-election next year. North American football chief Victor Montagliani is reportedly looking to challenge him.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told reporters that Mr Infantino was "the wrong man to lead the organisation".

FIFA had proposed creating a $US20 billion subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and its other events.

Thrive Eternal, a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, had been slated to lead the proposed investor group, according to FIFA. Joshua is the brother of Jared Kushner, who is US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Mr Trump and Mr Infantino have developed a close relationship, with the US co-hosting the recent 2026 World Cup.

President Trump said he had not spoken with Mr Infantino about the external investment plan.

ABC/Wires

title: Torquay netballers face decade wait for crucial facilities
text:
Before each home game, netballers from the Surf Coast Suns have to put up two large gazebos to be used as their change rooms.

Spectators are called to help wrestle with the structures at the Suns' notoriously windy home courts at the Banyul-Warri Fields in Torquay, and some players opt to get changed in their cars to avoid the hassle.

"In simple terms, it's horrible. The facilities for netballers are next to non-existent," player and under-19s coach Codi Emery said.

" The fact that we class a gazebo on game day as 'facilities' is outrageous. It's not good enough. "

Players who do not want to risk their privacy by using the gazebo have the option of using shared facilities 70 metres away.

Elisa Hall says it is hard to fully focus on playing netball when her belongings are not secure. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

A-grade co-captain Elisa Hall said not having a courtside change room and toilet was particularly tough for young players.

"They're still figuring out how long they can have a pad on or a tampon in without getting a leakage," she said.

"If they get one, they have to walk past a footy oval, in front of everyone and a bunch of strangers while bleeding."

Codi Emery says the Surf Coast Suns deserve better. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Emery said girls tended to drop out of sport when they were about the age of 14 or 15.

"We can obviously associate that with body changes," she said.

"How are we expected to encourage girls to stay in sport when we can't even give them a bit of privacy?"

The netballers are being asked to share a change room 70 metres from their courts. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Calls for council to step up

According to the Surf Coast Shire Council's social infrastructure plan, the club may have to wait up to 12 years for dedicated courtside change rooms, toilets, shelter, storage, drinking water, umpire and first aid facilities.

In the meantime, the council says the netballers can walk the 70 metres from the courts to nearby Grant Pavilion to access change rooms shared with football, hockey and soccer players.

Surf Coast Shire agrees its facilities need to be improved. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Hall said that simply was not workable.

"There was one Saturday where we shared that change room with the junior footy, the soccer, us, and our opposing team," she said.

"It's not ideal."

She said 70 metres might not seem far, but it was a long way for a young netballer at night.

"I can't trust my girls will be safe to go to the toilet during training," Hall said.

"It's a very open, communally used space … so you don't know who's going to be there."

The club's football president, Jay Williams, agreed.

"We don't have any line of sight to toilets or things like that, so it's a real safety concern," he said.

"We have girls and women getting changed in their car, which is pretty unacceptable in this day and age."

Jay Williams says netballers need access to better facilities. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Waiting a for decade or more

The Surf Coast Suns team was established 10 years ago as a junior club to absorb increasing demand in Torquay, one of the fastest-growing towns in Victoria.

This year the club fielded its first senior netball and football sides in the Bellarine league.

But as other sports in the town have grown, netball has seemingly been forgotten, Mr Williams said.

"The hockey club's just had a brand new pitch and they've got designs for brand new toilets, change rooms and admin rooms and netball's been left out," he said.

Surf Coast Shire is planning to extend a nearby basketball stadium in the next 10 or 12 years, which would include netball change rooms.

Chris Pike says several sporting clubs in the area want improved facilities. (Supplied: Surf Coast Shire Council)

The council agrees facilities need to be improved, but placemaking and environment general manager Chris Pike said there were "differing views on the best solution".

He said the council had been investigating whether the netballers could use the toilets at a nearby aquatic centre.

Playing catch-up

More than 1 million Australians play netball each year, making it the country's largest female team sport.

According to the Australian Sports Commission's AusPlay data, about a quarter of Australia's 14 million females participate in a sport-related activity at least once a week.

"All of a sudden female participation rates are booming and infrastructure decisions, which have been traditionally made around men, just haven't caught up," Deakin University associate professor Helen Brown said.

The Australian Sports Commission senior research fellow has surveyed 325 women about barriers to playing sport.

Helen Brown has surveyed hundreds of women about menstruation and sporting infrastructure. (Supplied: Deakin University)

"Most of them said they'd either missed a training session or a game because of inadequate facilities for their periods," Dr Brown said.

"They were really worried about 'what happens if I bleed and there's nowhere to go quickly' or if they're bleeding heavily, which is very prominent with a lot of young girls especially."

She said spaces for period care, breastfeeding and changing clothes were vital.

The Grant Pavilion at Banyul-Warri Fields opened 15 years ago. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

"Most community sporting facilities in Australia were built at a time when men's sport dominated everything from participation to membership and, as a result, all the change rooms and playing facilities are often just designed for men," Dr Brown said.

"Each state does have female-friendly guidelines for policymakers and councils to use.

"Whether or not they use them, I'm not sure."

A room with a door

On a dark and wet night water pools near the kit bags of the junior girls training for the Suns.

The netball courts the Surf Coast Suns train and play on. (ABC Geelong: Jonathon Kendall)

Emery says they're not asking for a lot.

"Just a simple change room — a room with a door that we can go into," she says.

"Just for privacy, so no-one can view us changing dresses.

"A tap to be able to fill up our water bottles would be fantastic, and the safety of walking to a toilet within 10 metres that's well lit and that isn't used predominantly by males."

title: Quick hits: Aussie walker's 'in your dreams champ' taunt before gold
text:
An Australian gold medallist refuses to be intimidated by his Kenyan rival, while an English weightlifter makes a stunning revelation ahead of her Celebrity MasterChef debut.

Here are the quick hits from day eight of the Commonwealth Games.

1. 'In your dreams champ'

Isaac Beacroft (left) exchanged words with Stephen Kihu during the men's 10,000m walk final. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Isaac Beacroft was not going to be told what to do in the men's 10,000m walk final.

The 19-year-old Australian stuck to his guns while exchanging words with Kenyan Stephen Kihu, whom he beat home for the gold.

"I knew he'd be there waiting for me to kick because he was taunting me the entire race, telling me to go around and lead it," Beacroft said.

"I was just saying, 'In your dreams champ, this is not happening today.'

"I knew he'd come back around me and then as soon as he did I thought I'd really drop the hammer and see if I could break him, and I did."

Beacroft added: "We were moving pretty quick at some stage and he was just telling me, 'Go around, go around.'

"I wasn't going to go around. I wanted it to be slow.

"You saw the kick that I had at the end, so I guess he backed himself at the end and so did I.

"If someone's going to give it to you, I'm going to give it back."

Isaac Beacroft refused to be told what to do by his Kenyan rival. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Beacroft was a member of Greater Western Sydney's junior academy until he was 16.

"I probably wasn't going anywhere in AFL, but I like to claim it," he said.

"I like to think I've made the right choice, especially when I'm about four-foot tall.

"I was usually just a step-ladder playing AFL."

2. Weightlifter's MasterChef reveal

English weightlifter Emily Campbell is also accomplished in the kitchen. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

As an Olympic and World Championships medallist, English weightlifter Emily Campbell knows a thing or two about dealing with pressure.

So it was no surprise when she won gold as favourite in the women's +86kg classification in Glasgow, setting a Games record (278kg) in the process.

But there is one stage Campbell admits she finds daunting: the Celebrity MasterChef set.

Campbell shifted from the weights room to the kitchen as a contestant in an upcoming series of the program in the UK.

"MasterChef was definitely more nerve-racking than this [Commonwealth Games], absolutely," Campbell told reporters.

"MasterChef was very tough. It was a very tough competition, but I enjoyed it thoroughly."

And what can viewers expect Campbell to cook up on Celebrity MasterChef?

"My signature dish is Caribbean, and that's all I'm going to give you because I want you to watch it," Campbell said.

3. Aussie pursuit women disqualified

Sophie Edwards was disqualified for an illegal addition to her helmet. (Getty Images: Sam Mellish)

One moment, 21-year-old Tasmanian Felicity Wilson-Haffenden was celebrating breaking the Australian 4,000m individual pursuit record and preparing to race again in the bronze medal race.

The next, she was staring, heartbroken, at the three letters no athlete wants to see on the official results next to her name: DSQ.

Both she and teammate Sophie Edwards were sensationally disqualified from the women's individual pursuit.

The official report stated that Edwards used "a helmet that has been altered or had any element added or removed in terms of design or form", while Wilson-Haffenden fell foul of a rule that prohibits riders from wearing clothing or any other accessory that could modify her morphology.

AusCycling executive general manager of performance, Jesse Korf, said Edwards had additional safety padding in her helmet and that she's "not upset".

He was not impressed about Wilson-Haffenden's disqualification, though.

"She's been seen by the medical team early this morning because of genuine shoulder discomfort and mobility issues," Korf said.

"Her shoulder got taped up to the middle of her [upper] arm

"On inspection after the race, the UCI concluded that the taping of the shoulder constituted a morphological change, but they weren't able to articulate what that exactly was because it's a grey area; you cannot measure what a morphological change is.

"Unfortunately, that conclusion is final, which we're most certainly not happy with. Felicity is upset, who is now our main concern."

4. Aussie's bronze at teammate's expense

Eliza Ault-Connell's crash in the first running of the women's 1500m T54 final prompted the re-run. (Getty Images: PA Images/Martin Rickett)

Someone was always going to be unhappy with the re-run of the women's 1,500 T54 race.

And it seems that Australian Mikaela Dingley copped the worst of it.

In the original race on Wednesday, Australian Eliza Ault-Connell and Mauritian world champion Noemi Alphonse were both taken out by Canadian Nandini Sharma.

She had gone on to finish second across the line, but was disqualified for causing the crash, which had promoted Australia's Dingley into the bronze medal position.

But because Australia and Mauritius protested the decision, authorities decided to re-run the race on Friday morning.

That proved a fateful decision, with the hampered athletes Alphonse and Ault-Connell going on to claim silver and bronze medals respectively.

"It's been an absolutely massive few days," the 44-year-old veteran told AAP.

"To have the opportunity to have this race re-run and for everyone to be able to go out there and put on their best in great conditions is really the outcome that all the athletes want."

Eliza Ault-Connell finished third in the re-run 1,500m race. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Perhaps not all the athletes.

The re-run meant that Dingley, who finished sixth in the re-run, was only bronze medallist for around 36 hours.

The silver medallist in the original race, England's Ellis Kottas, finished fourth in the re-run having told media she was "low-key traumatised" when she heard the race would be re-run.

"It's rough, but it is racing," Ault-Connell said.

"If she loves what she does and she continues to show up, it will happen.

"It's almost like 'cruel to be kind ', but we all go through that, and those opportunities are going to help you grow as an athlete."

Easy for her to say.

Somewhat pleasingly, Scottish athlete Melanie Woods won gold again, proving her result on Wednesday was no fluke.

5. Lawn bowler's 'once-in-a-lifetime opportunity'

Botswana's Charles Diteko hopes he can see Celtic play while he is still in Glasgow. (X)

Does Botswana's lawn bowler Charles Diteko have an ulterior motive for competing in Glasgow?

"I used to be a soccer player, and I'm a big fan of Celtic," Diteko said.

"So if there is a match on and I have time, I will try to get to it. It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity."

Of course, we're kidding.

We know his sole focus in Glasgow is competing for his country.

But Diteko may be in luck if he sticks around a day or so after Sunday's closing ceremony.

Celtic play Dundee in the Scottish Premiership on Monday night.

In the meantime, Diteko and Kaizer Geche are representing Botswana in the men's pairs competition.

title: Family's plea after daughter unable to donate organs
text:
John and Anne Apter say their daughter Sheridan was unapologetically herself, but also very generous with her time.

"There is no doubt whatsoever that if she could have helped someone, she would have said yes, 100 per cent," Mr Apter said.

But in the 35-year-old's final moments she was unable to give one last gift, and Australia's definition of death may have got in the way.

The last time Sheridan's parents saw her conscious was a family lunch that, typically, she had organised, before she left to spend the evening at a friend's place.

Sheridan Apter's parents say she was unapologetically herself and very generous with her time. (ABC News: Declan Bowring)

Later that night she was found unconscious and blue in the bathroom.

Sheridan was taken by ambulance to hospital and put on a ventilator in an intensive care unit at Sydney's St George Hospital.

Her family was told she had suffered severe brain damage from a lack of oxygen. Eight days later, they were informed her condition would not improve.

Mr and Mrs Apter knew Sheridan would like to donate her organs, so she was moved to a theatre in the hospital where surgeons waited as her life supports were removed.

Sheridan Apter's death is being investigated by the coroner. (Supplied: John and Anne Apter)

She continued to breathe and have a heartbeat for four hours. It meant her organs had deteriorated too much to be suitable to be used as transplants.

Her parents were devastated, having lost their daughter and knowing she wasn't able to donate her organs.

"I couldn't be more certain of anything in my life than what she would have wanted with her organs," Mr Apter said.

" She would have loved to go, 'Yep, yep. My heart's beating somewhere else.' "

The Apters want a discussion on how Australians could change the system so people like Sheridan could still donate their organs.

"If there is a way that those organs can be maintained … so that when that person finally passes away, the organs are still able to be donated, well, that would be magnificent," Mr Apter said.

John and Anne Apter want more of a discussion about increasing the possibility of organ donation. (Supplied: John and Anne Apter)

Laws on death

What may have prevented Sheridan from donating her organs is the way Australia defines death.

That definition under human tissue law says death is either the irreversible cessation of circulation of blood in the body or the irreversible cessation of all function of the brain.

Helen Opdam, national medical director with the Organ and Tissue Authority and an intensive care specialist, says no other country has that precise wording around blood circulation.

"Our wording in our legislation is very specific and fairly unique, and particularly the fact that we've got [the] wording irreversible cessation of circulation of blood in the body of the person," Dr Opdam said.

Helen Opdam says the way Australia defines death is relatively unique. (Supplied)

" For example, in the UK, they talk about permanent loss of consciousness and the capacity to breathe. That's their definition of death. "

Experts say Australia's definition prevents the use of modern technology that protects the organs from deterioration and increases their suitability for transplant.

Normothermic regional perfusion (NRP) is one method used in countries such as Spain, France and the UK. It restarts circulation to part of the body, as a form of organ support.

However, Dr Opdam said using NRP arguably invalidated the determination of death because of the restarting of circulation.

"It can be argued that if you restart blood flow to even just a part of the body of the person, the donor, the patient, then you're invalidating the criteria on which death was determined," she said.

Health ethics professor Dominique Martin, from Deakin University, said NRP could increase the number of organs donated.

A 2023 study in the United Kingdom found the number of organs able to be donated increased from 2.6 to 3.3 per donor when NRP was used.

"That might sound like sort of a small difference, but when you think about the number of DCD [donation after circulatory death] donors overall, it can make quite a big difference in terms of opportunities for transplant," Professor Martin said.

Dr Opdam said there were 2,000 people on the waitlist for an organ transplant, while just 557 people were able to donate organs last year, resulting in 1,438 people receiving donations.

She said there were also 14,000 people on dialysis, some of whom could benefit from a kidney transplant.

"The opportunity or the chance for donation is actually quite small," Dr Opdam said.

"In fact, any of us, we're all more likely to need a transplant in our lifetime than we are to die and be a donor."

Death definition under review

An Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) review of the death definitions is due to report to the federal Attorney-General on August 16.

A discussion paper released by the ALRC proposes a brain-based definition of death, which may open the door to NRP.

The paper explains that NRP is not used in Australia because it is considered inconsistent with the existing legal framework for determining death.

Dr Opdam says the definition of death was last done in Australia in 1977 and should be modernised.

"It's clear that our current human tissue acts need to be updated to reflect contemporary medical practices and understanding of death," Dr Opdam said.

Any change of laws would need to be done by the states and territories.

702 ABC Sydney approached the office of NSW Health Minister Ryan Park for comment, but our enquiry was redirected to the NSW health ministry.

"NSW has contributed to the Australian Law Reform Commission's review process and will carefully examine any findings or recommendations included in the final report," a spokesperson for NSW Health said.

More conversation about organ donation needed

While she wasn't able to give her organs, Sheridan's corneas were still able to be donated and restored sight in someone.

Her family has also continued her generous spirit in supporting the Confident Girls Foundation, which uses her beloved sport of netball to support girls from marginalised communities.

While the Apters were unaware of NRP at the time of Sheridan's death, they hope her story can spark discussion about increasing the possibility of organ donation.

That discussion during DonateLife week this week is timely as recent NSW figures show the number of registered donors has been falling.

Just 34,516 in NSW joined the Australian Organ Donor Register last year, a 19 per cent decrease from the year before.

"More lives could be saved if there was more of a discussion around exploring all the alternatives out there around organ donation and having more donors," Mr Apter said.

title: EPA recommends stricter pollution rules for Santos and Inpex
text:
The Northern Territory Environment Protection Authority (NTEPA) has recommended changes to the licences of Darwin's two major gas processing companies, Santos and Inpex, following a review triggered by substantial under-reporting of toxic emissions.

The report, released on Friday, calls for pollution limits, limits on hot venting, and continuous monitoring of emissions.

The review was launched after Inpex revealed it had drastically under-reported toxic emissions — including the carcinogen benzene — from its Ichthys LNG plant on Darwin Harbour, sparking concerns that residents and workers could be breathing in harmful emissions.

Santos's Darwin LNG tank is set to be filled again as part of the company's Barossa gas project. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

In March, independent consultants found widespread failures in how Inpex calculated and reported emissions dating back to the start of production in 2018.

Santos has also faced scrutiny over its Darwin LNG facility, where a leaking tank has released vast amounts of methane, and there has been frequent flaring.

The review follows months of criticism of the NTEPA's oversight and transparency from both members of the public and experts, including accusations the NTEPA has been "asleep at the wheel".

On Friday, NTEPA chairman Paul Vogel said the public should have confidence the regulator had their "health at heart" and insisted the recommendations would not be watered down by the companies.

Regulator in gas leak 'scandal' paid hourly rate by industry lobbyist The man in charge of the Northern Territory government's handling of a major methane leak at a Santos gas plant was working with a lobbyist for the project's co-owner.

Mr Vogel said while the review found the current environmental licences governing Santos and Inpex were among the strictest in the country, there was room for improvement.

He said the unusually close proximity of the facilities to Darwin city — around 6 kilometres away — and the likelihood of expansion "means that we really should have a world-class regulatory regime in place that goes further than we currently have".

"There's been independent health risk assessments conducted by the chief health officer to assure the community that their health is protected from [Inpex's] emissions," he said.

"But we need to make sure that continues in the future, and there's a lot more transparency around reporting and availability of information from the company to the community."

Regulation 'alarmingly slipshod'

Environment Centre NT climate campaigner Bree Ahrens welcomed action from the regulator, but said there were still "gaping holes in the recommendations" that would continue to put Darwin's air quality at risk.

"This review is an admission that the NT EPA's regulation of Inpex and Santos's toxic air pollution under the current licences has been alarmingly slipshod and needs to be fixed," she said.

NT EPA orders Santos, Inpex licence conditions review The Northern Territory environment regulator will re-examine the licence conditions of major gas facilities in Darwin, after one of its biggest operators admitted to under-reporting potentially toxic emissions at its Ichthys LNG plant.

Ms Ahrens said it was concerning the recommendations did not limit flaring or put a cap on how long acid gas incinerators — anti-pollution systems that burn harmful gasses at high temperatures before releasing them into the atmosphere — can be out of action.

Instead, the review recommends they are "operational" 99.5 per cent of the time.

"The effectiveness of this review will depend on its implementation," she said.

"The gas industry has shown again and again it can't be trusted when it comes to our air quality and health.

"The NTEPA needs to hold the line and impose the strongest possible licence conditions, with real consequences for non-compliance."

Other recommendations include expanding enforceable pollution limits, requirements to operate and maintain a "high level" of pollution control equipment, and regular audits.

Paul Vogel says the NT should have "a world-class regulatory regime in place that goes further than we currently have". (ABC News: Charlotte Hamlyn)

Documents submitted to a 2024 Senate inquiry revealed Inpex's incinerators had been out of service for extended periods since 2019.

title: How Gen Z sees money and how it drives their spending and saving
text:
Liam* was never taught how to manage money.

So, when he earned his first pay cheque at 16, keeping it was a challenge.

His purchases started small — treating himself to things he'd gone without growing up, like a steak at a restaurant.

Then the habits escalated — gaming consoles, online spending, takeaway.

His pay started to only last days.

"Tapping my card felt too easy because I never actually saw the money leaving my hand," he said.

Growing up in a financially unstable household where money was uncertain and rarely discussed, Liam entered adulthood without learning basic skills like budgeting or saving.

Watching his pay disappear reminded him of the instability he experienced as a child, when his financial security depended on someone else's decisions.

He realised he was repeating the pattern.

Liam spent the next six months consciously changing his habits, and by the end of it, he had almost $10,000 in the bank.

Gen Z savers, against the odds

Liam isn't alone.

Data from the NAB Wellbeing Survey Q1 2026 found young Australians aged 18-29 have the highest saving intention compared to older age groups.

In total, 94 per cent of Gen Z women were trying to save compared to 93 per cent for Gen Z men.

Both sat above the 81 per cent national average of all Australians putting money aside.

But Gen Z are also navigating a financial world that looks very different from previous generations — shaped by tap-and-go payments, buy now, pay later services, online ads and an endless stream of financial advice online.

So, how are young people managing their money?

To find out, we spoke to a few.

Hugo's parents gave him the freedom to manage his own money, but still encouraged him to save. (ABC News: Marc Eiden)

Hugo, 16. Supermarket worker.

Hugo works part-time at a supermarket and spends most of his pay on car modifications.

His understanding of money came from learning through trial and error.

"I sort of just started saving after realising I had no money left," he said.

His parents encouraged saving but left him to manage it. Hugo said he's better with money now but uncertain about the future.

" I don't feel 100 per cent confident I'll buy a house, but I'm hopeful. "

Bree says she feels confident managing her money because she has strong influences and support around her. (ABC News: Dimitria Panagiotaros)

Bree, 16. Fast food worker.

Bree spends most of her income on phone data and food, with the occasional splurge on music or gifts. She's saving for a car.

"I only spend what I know I can afford based on my shifts," she said.

Her parents taught her to budget using their own financial books.

"They really wanted us to learn from their mistakes."

Her mum can view her bank account but doesn't control it. She hopes to buy a house one day, though she worries about the current market.

Evelynn says whenever she has money, her mum reminds her not to blow it all. (ABC News: Amber Irving-Guthrie)

Evelynn, 16. Cello busker.

Evelynn earns money busking and spends most of it on social outings with friends.

She has her own bank account, but is still figuring out how to manage it.

"I feel like managing money is really stressful. I don't think most kids are very well educated on money," she said.

Evelynn has searched for advice online, like, 'How do I save money faster?' but felt she "never got a good answer on that".

When financial education falls short

Behind those different experiences is a common factor: not every young person starts with the same financial education or support.

Alyssia Kennedy, 29, runs the Life After School program, visiting Tasmanian high schools to teach students the practical money skills they're not getting in the classroom or at home, including tax, work rights and budgeting.

She said the demand told its own story.

"So many schools are reaching out saying, 'We need your help because we as teachers don't know these things either.'"

Ms Kennedy said the gap was generational.

Alyssia Kennedy founded the Life After School program to bridge educational gaps. (ABC News: Audrey Courty)

"People in their 50s and 60s were taught this, whether it was by mum and dad or through school," she said.

"But the curriculum has changed a lot since then. I'm seeing gaps with those whose parents are in their 40s or under."

"Some parents want to know how to have these conversations, while others don't have the knowledge themselves."

Ms Kennedy said what young people were spending on had not changed dramatically, but what had changed was their ability to access those things, making it easier than ever to spend without registering the cost.

Where Gen Z are getting their advice

When financial education is inconsistent, many young people are turning elsewhere for guidance.

The ASIC Moneysmart Gen Z Financial Behaviours Report 2026 found that 63 per cent of Gen Z use social media for financial guidance, while 52 per cent trust 'finfluencers' and 64 per cent trust AI platforms.

Nearly one in four own cryptocurrencies, with 29 per cent saying they trade based on social media or influencer recommendations.

Still, the data doesn't paint Gen Z as careless with money.

Sixty per cent also use professional sources for financial advice, while half turn to family and friends.

The findings suggest Gen Z is actively seeking financial information, but doing so through unregulated digital platforms, where algorithms can shape the content they see.

Nearly three in four Gen Z Australians saw ads encouraging cryptocurrency investment, while more than four in 10 were contacted directly by someone offering investment advice. (Adobe Stock)

Figuring it out anyway

For Liam, now 17, changing his financial habits meant rethinking his relationship with money.

He decided to put most of his pay aside in cash, limiting his access to digital spending. He cooked cheap meals and repaired things instead of replacing them.

"I realised that if I put a majority of it away in cash, it built up really quickly," he said.

For a generation raised on digital payments, tap and go has made spending faster and more convenient. (AAP: Dan Peled)

The almost $10,000 he saved bought a car, paid for a holiday, and helped him move out of home, things he said once felt out of reach.

Liam's story is one example of how Gen Z is learning how to manage money in a financial landscape unlike previous generations.

*Liam's name has been changed..

title: FIFA executive lashes Infantino over sell-off plan
text:
FIFA's chief operating officer said its staff were deceived by president Gianni Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan, and suggested the project must not go ahead.

Zurich-based executive Kevin Lamour all but invited Infantino to fire him in a statement to the Associated Press that defended his colleagues amid intense fallout from the FIFA boss's plan to sell stakes in future World Cup profits to private equity funds.

Mr Lamour wrote that staff were "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness in planning the sale over recent months and "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

"It is the project of one person," wrote Lamour, a long-time colleague of Infantino at both FIFA and European soccer body UEFA.

Gianni Infantino (left) and Donald Trump were often seen together during and in the lead-up to the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

"Not only must this project not go ahead … but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions."

Mr Lamour's statement came hours after Mr Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro, a former Goldman Sachs banker who represented the soccer body on the White House Task Force for the World Cup, resigned and urged other senior FIFA staff to speak out.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Mr Cordeiro wrote in a statement. The former US Soccer Federation president said he was not included in talks about the plan backed by a New York investment fund created by Joshua Kushner.

"Let me be clear. I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally," Mr Cordeiro said. He called the $US20 billion ($28.5 billion) commercial subsidiary "a bad deal for football".

Mr Lamour did not resign the post he has held since 2024 but said he had a duty to his colleagues.

Joshua Kushner (right) with brother Jared, is leading the charge to make a private investment in FIFA. (Getty Images: Patrick McMullan)

"And if that means I lose my job then so be it," the French official said.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

Mr Lamour came to soccer from politics two decades ago as an aide to then-UEFA president Michel Platini. He often had an international role in soccer politics, liaising with FIFA member federations in Africa and Asia, who are weighing their own decisions on Mr Infantino's offers of $US20 million each by a deadline of September 19.

Mr Cordeiro often joined Mr Infantino on working visits to meet US President Donald Trump at the White House in recent years.

"Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away," he said.

"That is why this proposal should be rejected."

Mr Infantino has proposed spinning off FIFA's commercial businesses — including World Cups and Club World Cups for men and women — into a $20 billion subsidiary with 20 per cent owned by private investors.

The "anchor investor," described by FIFA, is Kushner, the younger brother of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.

"FIFA already has access to extraordinary financial resources. The organisation sits on billions of dollars in reserves and no debt," Mr Cordeiro said. He noted FIFA's revenue of $15 billion in the past four years tied to the men's World Cup just ended.

A breakdown of FIFA's bid to sell the World Cup Gianni Infantino's plan to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to investors would grant them control over the World Cup.

"Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football's most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football's future without any compelling justification," he said.

Mr Cordeiro said he shared five years of working for FIFA alongside Infantino with "dedicated, principled people who care deeply about the game".

"I hope they, too, will speak up," he wrote, "because decisions of this magnitude should be made in the interests of football, not those who stand to profit from it."

Mr Infantino has been president of FIFA for more than 10 years and seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next March. FIFA has set a November 18 deadline for challengers to come forward.

Mr Lamour was part of Mr Infantino's inner circle that campaigned for him to become the surprise winner of that FIFA presidential election in February 2016.
