title: A breathalyser pregnancy test: How AI is sniffing out the next farming revolution
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsFederalAgriculture A breathalyser pregnancy test: How AI is sniffing out the next farming revolution Mike Foley August 1, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An electronic nose, powered by artificial intelligence, is helping Dr Bronwyn Darlington and her dairy cows, Soy and Oatley, to fit with the modern tastes in milk names, as Armadale, Flower, Pumpkin and Dixie sniff out the next revolution in global agriculture. Darlington and her Jersey herd are working on technology which promises to modernise farming techniques as old as agriculture itself with the Agscent sensor, like a breathalyser for cattle, which uses nano-sensors to detect chemical compounds in a cow’s breath at concentrations as low as parts per billion. Dr Bronwyn Darlington with her Jersey cows on the family farm in Carwoola, NSW. Alex Ellinghausen The breath analysis device can be used for a range of health-related applications, and a promising one is pregnancy detection, which can be confirmed as soon as 18 days after conception – weeks earlier than an invasive physical exam. This hands-off technique would replace the need for a veterinary test, using elbow-length gloves and a lot of invasive pushing and prodding, which is typically effective only after about 35 days.

Advertisement

Loading “Every time you bring an animal in and you do something invasive to it, you create a risk to the person, often a veterinarian, and a risk to the animal. But by doing a breath sample, it’s non-invasive and it gives you a really rich biological sample,” Darlington said. Related Article Biosecurity ‘Complacency crept in’: Australia defenceless against feral rabbit boom Significant advancements in agricultural productivity came in the “green revolution” of the 1960s, when new crop breeding techniques were deployed to produce high-yielding varieties of rice and wheat to feed the booming global population. More recently, the so-called agtech revolution in the 1990s used Global Positioning System (GPS) technology to boost yields by minutely tracking crops across fields and laser-guiding machinery to sow, till and harvest the field with precision.

Advertisement

Agscent uses electrodes coated with nanoparticles to identify a wide range of chemical compounds in an animal’s breath. AI and machine learning “decode” the information and can be trained to recognise the markers for bacteria, viruses and diseases. It can also identify imbalances in diet such as ketosis, which occurs when fat is burned instead of carbohydrates. Katie McRobert, director of the Australian Farm Institute think tank, said there was a deluge of new devices and technology applications promising to boost farmers’ bottom lines, but the problem was finding the time to learn how to use them. Darlington takes a breath sample from Soy, the Jersey cow. Alex Ellinghausen “AI can be a game-changer because the thing that makes farming difficult is the plethora of decisions that everybody has to get through on any given day,” McRobert said. “Australian farmers wear so many hats on any given day – they have to be an agronomist, a soil scientist, a livestock management specialist, an accountant.”

Advertisement

Despite these time pressures, technology developers often mistakenly assume that their products will prove popular if they can help farmers boost productivity, even if they take considerable time to learn how to use. This is where the addition of artificial intelligence is coming in. “AI can accelerate decision-making processes when given robust information and good guidelines to work within. It can speed up people’s learning and adoption of technology,” McRobert said. Dr Bronwyn Darlington with her Jersey cows on the family farm in Carwoola, NSW. Alex Ellinghausen Darlington said her Agscent product was like a space-age version of timeless technology.

“A dog can smell stress in humans or even cancer. A bull will jump through paddock fences to get to a cow. “Our technology simply means we can create a map of that, and if you can create a map of it, the task going forward is how many different productivity benefits can you get.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. “Ryan and Toby compete relentlessly. They’re consistent, disciplined, and that’s exactly what I value as a coach,” Young said. “I know how much these men care about the club, and they’ll play a huge role in helping us get to where we want to go.” Why Dragons axed five-eighth Atkinson for Dolphins clash Christian Nicolussi Daniel Atkinson’s fight to retain the St George Illawarra No.6 jersey has arrived more than six months early after the Dragons’ off-season recruit was dumped from the starting five-eighth role for Friday’s clash against the Dolphins. The Dragons signed playmaker Kodi Nikorima to a two-year deal on Wednesday. On Thursday, Atkinson was dropped to the extended bench for the first time this year and replaced by Lyhkan King-Togia.

Advertisement

Atkinson, 25, was the Dragons’ biggest off-season purchase, but he has struggled to make an impact, and coach Dean Young has opted for 21-year-old King-Togia instead. Moses Suli, who was named in the No.18 jersey, will start in the centres at the expense of Mat Feagai at WIN Stadium. “We let in two tries against the Warriors on our right edge, and we let in four tries against the Titans,” Young said. Daniel Atkinson will make way for Lyhkan King-Togia against the Dolphins on Friday. Getty Images “We know what Lyhkan brings with the ball – we need him to work hard defensively, and he gets his opportunity on Friday.” The Dragons have signed Nikorima, fellow playmaker Luke Metcalf, fullback Scott Drinkwater and prop Keaon Koloamatangi on multi-year deals, while Connor Watson will spend a season at the club on his way to the PNG Chiefs in 2028.

Atkinson was only a couple of years ago being groomed to take over from Will Kennedy at fullback at Cronulla, and one of the big talking points among fans this summer will be where he slots into the side with all the signings. When asked what the recruitment drive meant for Atkinson and halfback Kyle Flanagan, Young said: “What it means is we have good depth. I won’t dive into our recruitment strategy right now. At the moment we’ve got a panel that consists of [recruitment boss] Daniel Anderson, [CEO] Tim Watsford, [football operations boss] Ben Creagh and myself, and we have recruitment meetings every fortnight. Isaiya Katoa will return from injury against the Dragons. Getty Images “Things change really quickly in this game, as you know. As a club, we thought it was a great opportunity to bring in someone like Kodi with his skill set to improve our attack … we just have to focus on the rest of the year now.” Pressed on working with Atkinson, Young said: “He’s a competitor, he’s a great person, great trainer, he has a big, long kick on him – he’s done well for us this year at different stages, and he knows what he needs to work on, too.”

The Dolphins have also made changes in the halves. Coach Kristian Woolf confirmed Isaiya Katoa will return from a broken wrist, despite being named in the No.22 jersey. “He convinced us through the week he’s right to go, he’s done everything, and he’s been cleared medically,” Woolf said. “He’s a massive boost for us, he’s a class player and he’s a leader for us.” Woolf and Young have worked together with Tonga since 2019. Young confirmed he will step down from Woolf’s staff for the World Cup at the end of the year to focus on the Dragons. Even though the Dragons will collect the first wooden spoon in the joint venture’s history, the form of Hamish Stewart and Ryan and Toby Couchman has been a positive. With a number of injuries to Australian players, Young said Stewart would not look out of place in a Kangaroos jersey at the World Cup. Injuries to back row incumbents Angus Crichton and Hudson Young pave the way for the likes of Penrith’s Liam Martin, South Sydney’s Cameron Murray and Canterbury’s Jacob Preston to join Kevin Walters’ Australia squad. But Young believes Stewart, 21, would not disappoint.

“If you’re good enough, you’re old enough, that’s been proven over time, and Hamish Stewart is an elite player,” Young said. “He’s got a lot to learn, but to give you an insight of how talented he is, he never played back row until this year when I put him there. “I liked the way he moved defensively, and for the edges to defend well, you need four defenders to move well, and he moves really well. “He’ll end up being a ball-playing lock forward, but at the moment, but at his age, playing in the edge, it will be beneficial for him. “When you take squads away for tours and [World Cups], you need to make sure you have flexibility, and he definitely covers lock and back row. He’s got an elite skill set, and his work rate is outstanding.”

Roosters veteran prepared to entertain Super League move Christian Nicolussi Winger Daniel Tupou is leaning towards playing one more year with the Sydney Roosters, but should the Bondi club not accommodate him, he is prepared to pursue a two-year deal in the Super League. Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson on Tuesday confirmed Tupou would return for the NRL finals after dislocating his shoulder last Friday night against the Knights – but no call had been made about next year. Daniel Tupou is eyeing a Super League swansong. Getty Images

Advertisement

Tupou’s preference would be to play a 16th season in the red, white and blue. But the 35-year-old met his manager Sam Ayoub on Monday who informed him several English Super League clubs had expressed interest in him. The chance to sign a two-year deal has appeal, while Tupou also knows the Super League would be less physically demanding. Tupou remains one of the best aerial threats in the game, and bagged a hat-trick in his 300th milestone match against the Eels earlier this month. The Super League is known for its attacking brand of football, which would suit the Tongan international. Daniel Tupou receives his 300-game ball from recently departed NRL boss Andrew Abdo. Getty Images Mark Nawaqanitawase will leave the Roosters at the end of the season to return to rugby, and should Tupou also try his luck abroad, the Roosters have plenty of depth, including Cody Ramsey, Tommy Talau, Billy Smith, Manly recruit Reuben Garrick, and Tom Rodwell. They also have Rex Bassingthwaighte who is being groomed to be James Tedesco’s No. 1 successor, with the club happy to give their future fullbacks time on the wing at the start of their careers.

Advertisement

Tupou has never wanted any fuss made about his achievements, and played down the extent of his injury early in the second half in Newcastle last week. Tedesco said on Sunday: “The other night he laid on the floor and said, with no emotion, ‘My shoulder’s out’. That was it. “We all went up to him, but he was his usual calm self. They popped it back in, he was still out there, and I started to think he was going to keep playing, but they took him off. “Players get older and you expect a bit of a dip [in form], but that’s not the case with ‘Toops’ – he goes about his business with no fuss and we have so much confidence and belief when he’s out there.”

Advertisement

The setback means Tupou, who has played 302 matches for the club, is no chance to overtake Jared Waerea-Hargreaves as the most-capped Rooster should this year be his last. Waerea-Hargreaves played 310 games, and with the Roosters to play six regular season games, and potentially up to three finals, Tupou could have moved to 311. Robinson confirmed Tupou would return for the finals, and the shoulder injury would sideline him between four and six weeks. As for his future, Robinson said: “I’d say it’d be in the next two to three weeks, we’ll know where ‘Toops’ is at and where we’re at.” Young weighs up Raiders’ deal Dan Walsh

Canberra have offered Hudson Young a multimillion-dollar, three-year extension as his Raiders teammate Morgan Smithies will join Perth next season. The Raiders have progressed negotiations with Young after he was sidelined with a season-ending Achilles injury last weekend, and are gunning to keep their star NSW back-rower off the open market on November 1. Loading A three-year deal would keep Young in the nation’s capital until the end of 2030. With the NRL’s salary cap forecast to rise to at least $15 million from 2028, Young’s total extension is expected to be worth around $3 million and make him one of the game’s best-paid back-rowers. Along with Penrith enforcer and Blues teammate Liam Martin, Young is the most accomplished edge forward coming off-contract in 2027.

Advertisement

Young’s Achilles rupture came as a cruel blow to Canberra’s late-season finals charge given the 28-year-old’s superb Origin campaign and status as a nailed-on World Cup starter for the Kangaroos. Canterbury’s Jacob Preston (24), Wests Tigers’ Samuela Fainu (22) and the Dolphins’ recent Queensland Origin debutant Kuikefu Finefeuiaki (22) represent the next crop of back-rowers yet to be tied down long-term, though the Tigers’ plans to present Fainu with an upgraded deal were a significant factor in Jarome Luai being released early to join Parramatta next year. Hudson Young in action for Canberra. Getty Images Martin’s agent will meet with the Panthers this week as the club works through its star-studded off-contract list, with co-captains Nathan Cleary and Isaah Yeo the club’s retention priorities. Martin and Brian To’o have both been linked to the incoming PNG Chiefs franchise, and while Penrith will be given first and last rights on Martin’s future, a request for permission to negotiate early with rival clubs hasn’t been ruled out, either.

Teammate Moses Leota was granted a brief window to talk to rivals by the Panthers last month to get an idea of his market value. Related Article NRL 2026 The Tigers said Doueihi talks were ‘positive’. What happens next will tell the real story Melbourne have also given five-eighth Cameron Munster permission to negotiate specifically with PNG after undergoing minor knee surgery, though the Storm have tabled a two-year extension for 2028-29 at a reduced rate from his estimated $1.25 million salary. The Chiefs are unlikely to present their own offer until November 1, or when there is clarity around Cleary’s future given he is their preferred playmaking target. Smithies, meanwhile, has agreed to terms on a three-year offer from Perth. The 25-year-old had been deep in negotiations with Canberra earlier this year before the club was told his preference was to move back to the UK and resume his English Super League career.

Perth’s offer proved too good for Smithies to refuse, but the English international will leave the Raiders on good terms despite the change of plans. The Bears have also targeted Eels co-captain Junior Paulo as a potential captaincy option for inaugural coach Mal Meninga next season, with a two-year offer expected to be taken up by the veteran prop this week. Perth have slowly but surely built a robust pack with Penrith’s Liam Henry and Scott Sorensen, Cronulla utility Siosifa Talakai and Bulldogs back-rower Josh Curran their most notable signings up front. Updated SportSoccerFIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino Updated August 1, 2026 — 12:39pm ,first published August 1, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has scrapped his controversial plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Facing backlash throughout the sport, a World Cup boycott from Europe and criticism from high-ranking officials inside FIFA itself, Infantino said the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise project “will not proceed.” Under pressure: FIFA President Gianni Infantino. Getty Images The news came Friday night (Saturday morning AEST) with the governing body releasing a statement “attributable to the FIFA President.” “The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed,” the statement read.

Advertisement

“And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders. View post on X “Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place. “Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. “As a result, this proposal will not proceed.”

Advertisement

The statement ended with Infantino saying he plans to “bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks” with the goal of discussing ways to grow the sport of soccer globally. Carlos Cordeiro, pictured in 2019. AP Photo/CHARLES REX ARBOGAST Infantino’s concession concluded a tumultuous week. The proposal was introduced just Tuesday, with FIFA projecting tens of billions in new investment by bringing together its commercial rights – encompassing broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing – under a new commercial venture and selling stakes in that venture to private equity. Infantino had defended his plan as beneficial for member nations that could access increased development money. FIFA also argued that outside investors wouldn’t have an operational role in the tournament and would invest in a subsidiary rather than FIFA itself. That didn’t soften what many saw as an attempt to hand minority ownership in the world’s biggest tournament to private investors with their own aims.

Advertisement

Member nations of UEFA (Europe’s governing body) voted to boycott World Cups moving forward if the plan went through. Members of CONCACAF, representing North America, Central America and the Caribbean, also “unequivocally” rejected the proposition. Carlos Cordeiro, the senior adviser to Infantino for the past five years, resigned earlier in the day in protest of the FIFA Forward Enterprise plans. Cordeiro, 70, is the former president of US Soccer (2018-20) and a Goldman Sachs banker before that. “Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA’s Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game,” Cordeiro wrote in a lengthy statement concerning his resignation. “Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away. That is why this proposal should be rejected.” Cordeiro pointed out that FIFA “sits on billions of dollars in reserves” and carries no debt as an organisation.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup FIFA’s offering Australia $45m to back selling the World Cup. Saying no might not be easy “If Member Associations believe additional investment is needed to develop the game, FIFA already has the financial capacity to provide that support from its existing resources,” Cordeiro said. “Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football’s most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification.” Meanwhile, the chief operating officer of FIFA also blasted Infantino’s desire to introduce private investors into the tournament’s financing, calling it “the project of one person.” Kevin Lamour said in a statement to the Associated Press that staff inside FIFA felt “deceived” by Infantino and the opaque nature of the process, adding they “deserve better than contempt and intimidation.” “It is the project of one person,” Lamour wrote. “Not only must this project not go ahead ... but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions.”

Advertisement

The Frenchman went on to add, “And if that means I lose my job then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision. At least I’ll sleep well tonight.” Lamour campaigned for Infantino in the 2016 FIFA presidential election. Reuters Sports news, results and expert commentary. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

Exclusive SportNRLNRL 2026 Secret clause in NRL TV deal lays bare motivation to add 20th team by 2029 Adrian Proszenko August 1, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL has a $120 million incentive to introduce a 20th team due to a secret clause in its $5.3 billion broadcast deal as the game’s desire to expand is set to deliver a new franchise by the end of the decade. Rugby league is in strong financial health after brokering the deal last month with Foxtel and Nine, the publisher of this masthead. The seven-year agreement runs from 2028 to 2034, making it the largest media rights package in Australian sports history. However, sources not authorised to speak publicly due to commercial sensitivities have told this masthead that $20 million per season will be deducted from the deal from 2029 onwards if a 20th team isn’t added to the competition. That would amount to a total of $120 million for the final six years of the arrangement. The Perth Bears will become the 18th team in 2027 and the Papua New Guinea Chiefs the 19th the following year. There isn’t a definitive call on if and where a new franchise will be added in 2029.

Advertisement

But given the governing body’s desire for growth - and the huge financial incentive to do so - it’s expected further expansion will occur. It’s also an indication that broadcasters are prepared to pay for an additional game each week. A second team in New Zealand is the most likely scenario, although the NRL hasn’t ruled out the prospect of a fifth Queensland team. By going to 20 teams, the NRL will have more flexibility around its draw, raising the prospect of a conference system and a more strategic placement of byes, including a concentration of them in the middle of the season. Warriors fans look on during the round 16 NRL match between New Zealand Warriors and North Queensland Cowboys at One NZ Stadium in Christchurch in June. Getty Images The Warriors have made huge inroads in rugby-mad New Zealand, playing in front of packed crowds. However, there is a feeling the nation has the talent, infrastructure and interest to accommodate a second side. The Southern Orcas are a Christchurch-based bid team attempting to win the next NRL licence.

Advertisement

“We’re doing our best to ensure that is the outcome,” said Southern Orcas chairman Graham Lowe. “It’s a fantastic opportunity for rugby league in the epicentre of rugby union, you can’t overlook that fact. “The Warriors have done a fantastic job in a rugby union country, where rugby union is the national sport. But the popularity of the NRL is phenomenal. “You can go anywhere in New Zealand and for younger people, the NRL is right at the front of their mind. The excitement you can feel in the south isle about a new team coming in in Christchurch, it’s fantastic.” The Orcas propose to play out of One NZ Stadium, a 30,000-seat venue with a glass roof that was opened this year. “It’s made for the NRL,” Lowe said. “It’s absolutely perfect conditions for every single game. It’s walking distance from the CBD and is made for entertainment.”

Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 NRL to road-test controversial kick-off rule change in ‘dead rubber’ matches Some pundits have questioned whether there’s enough talent to spread across another team. However, Lowe is adamant New Zealand is a huge pipeline for aspiring rugby league players. “There’s miles of talent over here,” he said. “The Warriors have done a fantastic job, but they are just one team. This offers opportunities to young kids who start college and have been besotted and brainwashed by rugby union. “This offers them an opportunity right on their doorstep. We want to get them from the cradle. “Rugby league has copped the rough end of the pineapple in this country for as long as I can remember and all the prized possessions of rugby union have evolved in Christchurch. We’re going to wear some hobnailed boots among that lot.”

title: ‘Fill in the blank’: Why Australian sprint star had nothing to say about 200m gold medallist
text:
Advertisement

Glasgow: Australian sprint champion Torrie Lewis says she was told not to speak out about banned sprinter Adaejah Hodge, who won gold in the 200 metres at the Commonwealth Games but was only running in the race after her suspension for doping was discounted twice. Lewis came sixth on Saturday morning (AEST) behind Hodge, an athlete from the British Virgin Islands whose four-year ban was first reduced to two years, and then by a further seven months, by the Athletics Integrity Unit. Adaejah Hodge (centre) crossed the finish line ahead of Australia’s Torrie Lewis (left). Getty Images Hodge was originally banned after winning the 2024 world under-20 championships in Peru – a suspension that eventually meant Lewis was promoted from silver to gold. Watching Hodge be given permission to compete and win in Glasgow was galling for Lewis, who has previously said “anyone who has a drug charge against them will always have a taint to their name and some suspicion that come with that”.

Advertisement

The AIU announced Hodge’s reduced penalty in March. View post on X Asked about Hodge in Glasgow, Lewis said: “I’ve been told not to say anything of that. I would love to say some words, but not allowed to. “I think everyone knows what I would like to say, but yeah, just fill in the blank yourself.” Lewis won 100m bronze in an Australian record time earlier in the week. Getty Images

Advertisement

Lewis didn’t appear alone in her thoughts on Hodge. The other runners didn’t embrace her or shake her hand at the finish line. Hodge said she didn’t care what “haters” thought. “It [the last year] hasn’t been stressful. I put all that behind me. It is what it is,” she said after her win. “Things happen and I just wanted to move forward and see what I can do, work extra hard and show that I didn’t need it [performance-enhancing drugs]. I never will need it. I knew I had to put in extra work to prove to the haters that I am Adaejah Hodge. Hodge with her gold medal for the 200m. Getty Images

Advertisement

“It’s competition. Our goal out here is to win. I don’t really know what to say about that. It’s about competing. If you want to shake my hand, shake my hand. If you don’t, don’t. I’m gonna be a good sport and tell everybody good job.” Shaniqua Bascombe from Trinidad and Tobago, who won silver, said she didn’t pay attention to what other athletes did. Did she have faith Hodge was clean? “No comment. I don’t know what to say.” Loading

Advertisement

Hodge was initially given a four-year ban for taking a prohibited substance but had it reduced to two years when the AIU accepted her explanation that the doping was not intentional, and she had not deliberately administered the substance. Two other athletes from the Montverde Academy in Florida where Hodge trained also tested positive to the same drugs in a 12-month period, prompting an investigation and then charges against the head coach Gerald Phirri. Hodge’s drug ban was kept confidential by the AIU, against its regular policy, because it said making the ban public could have jeopardised an important ongoing investigation. She was given an additional seven-month discount, leaving her free to compete in Glasgow, because of her “substantial assistance” in an investigation. Despite the situation, Lewis was pleased with her sixth place. Related Article Commonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal

Advertisement

“It wasn’t bad, you know. Considering this whole championships, I’m really proud that I made the final of this, and tried to put up a good fight,” she said. “If you would have told me at the start of this competition, would I be happy with sixth? I would have said absolutely. So I think after the 100 [final, where she won bronze] I just put my expectations even higher of myself, so I just still need to remind myself that you know, it was a big goal of mine to even make this final. So I’m still happy with that.” ‘Of course I’m disappointed’ It was a weird mixed feeling that Nina Kennedy could relate to. She won silver in the women’s pole vault but came away, disappointed – not only that she didn’t win gold, but more that she made mistakes and only jumped 4.65m. “I’m disappointed. Of course, I’m disappointed. I wanted to win, and I didn’t, and that’s OK,” she said.

Advertisement

She added: “I don’t think I’ve jumped that low (4.65m) in like four years, and I think that just demonstrates how tough it was. I know I’m in better shape than that.” In cold conditions, with gusty crosswinds, the world and Olympic champion struggled to find any rhythm. New Zealand’s Eliza McCartney, an Olympic bronze medallist who held the Oceania record of 4.94m until Kennedy broke it last month, beat the Australian on a countback, having not missed a height until 4.70. Kennedy missed at 4.65m. “You know, I’m superhuman most of the time, but I’m also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes. “I’m a really good hot-weather jumper, but clearly I’m not a very good cold-weather jumper, and I’ll wear that.

Advertisement

“That amazing tailwind that the sprinters have been getting – that’s been like a complete crosswind for us. So it was so cold out there, but that’s a part of it. And Eliza did better. She handled the conditions better, and that’s why she’s walking away with gold.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Gold for 19-year-old Aussie in the race walk, Australia sweep the podium in cycling ‘I gave it my best shot’ Sprinter Lachie Kennedy, who won silver and broke the national record in the 100m earlier in the week, had a similar night to Lewis, both showing perhaps the fatigue of racing day after day. Kennedy finished sixth in the men’s 200m final.

Advertisement

“Hey, I gave it my best shot but they gave it a crack. I came away injury-free. It was f--king cold out there,” he said. “I think we needed an Aussie in the final to show that we’re one of the best sprinting nations in the world. So I had to go out and represent. I probably didn’t perform as good as I would have liked, but I can’t be too upset, you know. I’m happy.” For Sarah Billings it took two world champions to beat her in the 800m. Billings won bronze just 0.03 seconds behind Kenya’s Lilian Odira, the reigning world champion. England’s Georgia Hunter-Bell, the world indoor champion who won silver outdoors at last year’s world championships behind Odira, took gold. That is the company Billings is now in, at the line with the two best women in the world. “I can’t believe it that I’m on the podium with them, and they’re just incredible athletes. And now I’ve just got to believe that I am too,” said Billings.

title: FIFA abandons World Cup privatisation plan after fierce backlash
text:
In brief FIFA planned to create a commercial subsidiary that would run its main events, including the World Cup, which private investors could buy stakes in.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino announced on Saturday the plan was being scrapped.

FIFA has abandoned plans to sell a stake in the World Cup after fierce backlash, including threats of boycotts.

In a statement on Saturday morning, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said it had "become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place".

"Our purpose has always been — and will always be — to unite and improve," he said.

"As a result, this proposal will not proceed.

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game, and with the objective to continue growing football everywhere, particularly in those countries that mostly need our support."

FIFA on Wednesday announced its plan to create a commercial subsidiary known as the FIFA Forward Enterprise that would run its main events, including the World Cup.

Private investors would have been able to buy a minority stake of up to 20 per cent in the subsidiary, which was valued up to US$20 billion ($28.47 billion).

FIFA had promised each of its 211 member countries and territories US$40 million ($56.9 million) in funding for the 2027-2030 cycle if they agreed to the plan.

But the backlash to the proposal was fierce, with the 55 member states of the European football governing body UEFA voting unanimously to boycott all FIFA tournaments.

Other bodies also opposed the plan, including CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, as did the Asian Football Confederation, of which Australia is a part of.

The plan also exposed internal division within FIFA.

Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned and called the plan a "bad deal for football", while FIFA chief operating officer Kevin Lamour said staff had been "deceived" by Infantino and the proposal was a "project of one person".

title: Why Australia ships out its wealth — and buys it back as finished goods
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Every day, bulk carriers leave Australian ports carrying iron ore, lithium, bauxite and other minerals bound for factories across Asia, Europe and North America.

Many of those same resources return months later as cars, batteries, solar panels, household appliances and electronics — finished products that capture far more value than the raw materials Australia exported.

The picture is a far cry from the one first promoted by the 'Australian Made' campaign of the 1980s. Launched by the then-Hawke government in 1986, along with its now ubiquitous logo, Australian Made projected a vision of a thriving domestic manufacturing industry — one that has never quite come to pass.

For decades, Australia has instead built much of its prosperity by exporting what it digs out of the ground. It is the world's largest exporter of iron ore and one of the world's leading producers of critical minerals needed for the global energy transition. Yet manufacturing today accounts for a relatively small share of Australia's economy compared with many other advanced nations, while many of the consumer and industrial goods Australians use every day are imported.

The debate over what Australia should make has returned to the spotlight this week, however, after the federal government announced a pre-feasibility study into what could become Australia's first new large-scale oil refinery in six decades, as part of a broader push to strengthen domestic industrial capability and fuel security.

The proposal also builds on the Albanese government's Future Made in Australia policy, which aims to expand local manufacturing and processing in industries including renewable energy and critical minerals.

The government's renewed focus on the sector comes as international conflicts continue to disrupt global supply chains — echoing vulnerabilities exposed during the COVID-19 pandemic, which prompted governments around the world to reassess their reliance on foreign imports

Against that backdrop, Australia now faces a question that reaches beyond the factory floor: should the country continue to focus on exporting its raw materials, or use them to produce more of the products Australians need?

The decline of mass manufacturing

For much of the post-World War Two period, manufacturing was one of the pillars of the Australian economy. Protected by high tariffs and supported by a growing population, factories produced everything from cars and white goods to textiles, steel and household appliances, employing more than one in five Australian workers by the early 1970s.

Holden ended 69 years of local vehicle manufacturing in Australia when it officially closed its Elizabeth assembly plant in South Australia in 2017. Source: AAP / Mark Brake

That started to change in the decades that followed. As trade barriers fell, production shifted overseas and the economy became dominated by services and mining. In turn, manufacturing steadily shrank as a share of both employment and economic output.

While the decline unfolded over decades, it became most visible through the closure of major factories and the industries that once formed the backbone of Australian manufacturing.

The shutdown of car manufacturer Holden's Elizabeth plant in South Australia in 2017 became a defining symbol of that change, ending more than seven decades of domestic car production and closing one of the country's most recognisable manufacturing operations.

Data reflects the trend, too. According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS), manufacturing's share of gross domestic product (GDP) has fallen from around 14 per cent in the mid-1970s to about 5 per cent in 2025, while its share of employment has declined from more than 20 per cent of the workforce to around 6 per cent over the same period.

Despite this, Australia retains manufacturing capability across several key sectors, including food and beverages, medical technology, specialist machinery, mining equipment, chemicals and defence-related industries. Together, these industries contribute $141.97 billion in industry value added to the Australian economy, according to ABS data.

Source: SBS News

The decline has also occurred in other advanced economies. Countries including the United States, the United Kingdom and Japan have seen manufacturing account for a smaller share of economic activity over recent decades as services have expanded and consumption patterns have changed.

Economist Saul Eslake says Australia's smaller manufacturing footprint also reflects the structure of the economy itself, particularly the size of its resources sector.

"If Australia has a bigger mining sector than any other 'advanced' economy except Norway — which we do, because nature has endowed this country with unusually rich and varied mineral resources — then it is a matter of arithmetic, not economic policy, that some other sector or sectors will be smaller in Australia than in other economies," he tells SBS News.

"Manufacturing is one of those."

How mining reshaped Australia's economy

Over the same period that manufacturing's share of the economy declined, the resources sector expanded to become one of the country's most important economic engines.

Mining has long been a major part of the economy, supported by large reserves of iron ore, coal, natural gas, and, more recently, critical minerals, including lithium.

In 2024-25, the industry contributed $260.57 billion in industry value added to the economy.

Australia is now one of the world's largest exporters of these commodities, supplying resources to markets including China, Japan, South Korea and other trading partners.

Source: SBS News

Economists say the rise of the resources sector has also shaped discussions around whether Australia can capture more value from the commodities it produces, particularly as demand grows for critical minerals used in technologies such as batteries, renewable energy systems and specialised manufacturing.

Emeritus professor Roy Green, a special innovation adviser at the University of Technology Sydney who specialises in advanced manufacturing, says Australia's strengths extend beyond resource extraction, particularly in industries that combine engineering and manufacturing expertise.

"Certainly, medical manufacturing, some areas of precision engineering, mining equipment, energy supply chains, construction materials and a handful of consumer goods, exemplified by Røde microphones. Plus food and wine," he says.

The push to move further into processing and higher-value production has grown as demand for critical minerals increases.

READ MORE The Australian first that could save thousands worldwide

Green says Australia has the resources to capture more value, but faces challenges in competing globally.

"That's a big question, and we could do it tomorrow and capture more of the final value, but to do it in a way that's environmentally acceptable would make processing uncompetitive unless it gets subsidised.

"[But] are we up for massive subsidies, or is there a way we can use technologies such as AI to make processing competitive in global markets?"

The scale problem: Why Australia finds it harder to compete

Manufacturing is not only about having the resources or the technical ability to produce something. Economists say it also depends on scale — the ability to spread the cost of factories, equipment, research and skilled labour across enough production to compete internationally.

Countries with large domestic or integrated markets have a built-in advantage. The US, China, Japan and the European Union can support large manufacturing industries because companies can access large pools of consumers, either within their own markets or through closely connected trading relationships.

Australia faces different conditions due to its smaller population and geographic distance from major consumer markets, which adds costs for businesses competing in global supply chains.

According to ABS data, around 868,000 Australians are employed in the manufacturing sector, representing about 5.9 per cent of the national workforce. Credit: Supplied

Eslake says manufacturing scale is usually achieved in one of two ways: through a large domestic market or through access to large export markets.

"Either you have a big domestic market as the US, the EU, China, Japan and Brazil do and India and Indonesia potentially do; or alternatively you get 'scale' by exporting to large markets, as Japan did after the Meiji Restoration in 1873 [Japan's 19th-century industrialisation period] and again after World War Two, and as Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Canada, Mexico, Ireland, Sweden, Switzerland and Türkiye, also a fairly large domestic market, have done," he says.

But notice that all of these second group of countries are geographically close to large markets, which we are not, and we don't have a large domestic market.

What should Australia manufacture in the future?

The debate over Australia's manufacturing future is no longer only about whether factories can return. It is about which capabilities matter most in an economy that will continue to rely on global trade.

The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the risks of relying on global supply chains, as disruptions exposed vulnerabilities across industries.

Raelene Lockhorst is the deputy director of the National Security Program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, specialising in areas including geopolitics and supply chains. She says the experience during COVID changed the way governments and businesses think about manufacturing capability.

"COVID-19 exposed the risks of Australia's reliance on highly efficient but fragile global supply chains. It demonstrated that access to essential goods cannot always be guaranteed during a crisis and reinforced the need to balance economic efficiency with resilience, sovereign capability and supply-chain diversity," she tells SBS News.

But experts say rebuilding the industries Australia once relied on is unlikely to be practical or economically efficient. Instead, the debate has shifted towards which new industries Australia should support, with the government's Future Made in Australia policy placing a renewed focus on domestic manufacturing.

Richard Holden, vice-chancellor's professor and chief societal economist at the University of New South Wales, argues the focus should be on identifying industries where dependence on overseas suppliers could create serious risks.

I think the Future Made in Australia policy is misguided, because it doesn't provide a framework for thinking about what we should and shouldn't do.

"For instance, even the US can't compete with China on electric vehicles, so do we think Australia does?" he tells SBS News.

Holden says the challenge is deciding where Australia needs to maintain its own industrial capability and where it can rely on international suppliers.

"We need to think about what we can buy on global markets and 'friend-source' and then what is really critical that we can't easily buy," he says.

He says the government's focus on the employment potential of manufacturing, outlined in its Future Made in Australia policy, does not necessarily mean those industries are strategically important.

Lockhorst says Australia should focus on retaining capability in areas where manufacturing is economically and nationally important.

"Australia shouldn't attempt to rebuild every industry, but focus on capabilities critical for national resilience, such as defence manufacturing, critical minerals processing, energy infrastructure, agricultural inputs and advanced manufacturing," she says.

Source: SBS News

Can Australia become a manufacturing nation again?

While Australian manufacturing is unlikely to return to the factory floors of the past, there is still a substantial workforce sustaining the industry.

According to ABS data, around 868,000 Australians are employed in manufacturing, underscoring that the sector remains a significant source of jobs and industrial expertise.

For manufacturers already operating in Australia, the future of the sector is less about competing on low costs and more about producing specialised, high-value products.

One example is ANCA Pty Ltd, an Australian company that designs and manufactures computer numerical control grinding machines used in precision manufacturing industries around the world.

Edmund Boland, CEO of ANCA, believes the broader industry should focus on maintaining the skills, knowledge and innovation systems that allow companies to develop complex products.

Edmund Boland, CEO of ANCA, says Australia is unlikely to compete globally on the basis of scale or low labour costs. Credit: Supplied

"Bringing engineering and manufacturing together enables faster problem-solving, stronger collaboration and a direct connection between product design and production. Australian engineers are highly creative and capable of solving complex problems, and this is reflected in the innovative, high-value products ANCA develops for global markets," Boland tells SBS News.

Boland points to the challenges Australia faces competing with countries that have better access to global markets.

Australia is unlikely to compete internationally through scale or low labour costs.

"We can compete through advanced technology, automation, intelligent business systems, specialist skills and the ability to produce complex, high-value products," he says.

Experts say Australia should prioritise industries where local production is critical. Credit: Supplied

Experts broadly agree that Australia now needs to be selective about the industries it supports, focusing on areas where losing local production capacity could create serious risks.

The goal is not for everything to be Australian-made, Lockhorst explains, but rather ensuring Australia retains the skills, infrastructure and industrial capacity needed when global disruptions occur.

Australia should not pursue complete self-sufficiency, but it must build resilience in areas where dependence creates unacceptable strategic risks.

"The goal should be maintaining sovereign capability in critical sectors, diversifying supply chains through trusted partnerships and ensuring Australia retains the skills, infrastructure and industrial capacity needed when global systems are disrupted."

title: 'Means so much to me': A different side of Bluey is taking centre stage

IN BRIEF The opening night of Garma Festival will feature a community screening of Bluey episodes in Yolŋu Matha language.

Five episodes have been translated into Yolŋu Matha and voiced by local Yolŋu community members.

Garma Festival gathers the best and brightest to Gumatj Country every year — and this year there's an extra special guest.

Australia's favourite dog, Bluey, has her paws on the red dirt and is cuddling up with the crowds in a special celebration of the show's recent Yolŋu Matha episodes.

Premiered during NAIDOC Week, five episodes of the iconic children's cartoon were translated to Yolŋu Matha and voiced by Yolŋu community members.

In celebration, Garma Festival will screen the episodes on site on Friday night, with the guest of honour in attendance.

For young Gika Yunupingu, it's a very exciting day.

"I like Bluey," he told NITV.

Gika Yunupingu took the opportunity to get a photo with one of his favourite cartoon characters. Source: AAP / James Ross

"Having Bluey here has made everyone excited," his dad Winston Yunupingu said.

"Everyone is excited to see her and to get around her and be together."

He believes the Yolŋu Matha episodes will do his community proud.

"It's very important for the kids here, and the ones that are coming up. It's important for non-Indigenous kids to watch as well and to learn about Gove," he said, referencing the Gove Peninsula, where Garma is held.

Kenisha Black is in her senior years at high school. But she's just as much a fan of Bluey as the younger kids.

Being able to watch Bluey in Yolŋu Matha gives her a deep sense of pride in her culture and language.

"It means so much to me, and it makes me so proud," she said.

"I'm glad the young kids have it. I wish I had it when I was younger."

For Lulu Sutherland, the translated episodes are a meaningful step in the sharing of Yolŋu culture with the nation.

"It's really good having Bluey in Yolŋu Matha because all the local kids can watch it in their own language, without having to translate it into English," she said.

"Yolŋu culture is really important for this world ... if it is shared across Australia that will be for the better."

'Bluey has become a shared language'

The translated episodes are the result of a partnership between Yolŋu Radio, the Aboriginal Resource Development Services (ARDS), the Australian Broadcasting Association and Ludo Studio.

title: Census 2026 guide: When is Census night and everything you need to know
text:
Every five years, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) counts every person and every household in the country as part of the Census of Population and Housing.

That includes Australians, young and old, from metropolitan and rural Australia. Even holidaymakers, international students and temporary visa holders are counted. It's often referred to as the most comprehensive snapshot of Australia, akin to a family photograph of the country.

This year, the Census will take place on Tuesday 11 August.

In the lead-up to Census night, here are all your questions answered.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

How do you complete the Census?

From late July, households will receive instructions on how to complete the Census. Australians can complete the form as soon as they receive instructions, provided they know where they will be on Census night.

Most people will receive a letter with instructions to complete the Census online. However, Australians can also request a paper form if they prefer.

The Census form is available in English. The ABS provides translated information and interpreting services for different languages. Source: Supplied / Australian Bureau of Statistics

Generally, one person per household will complete the Census, but separate forms can be requested for privacy reasons.

What is Census data used for?

Census data is used to inform decisions about language services, settlement support, transport, schools, health care, infrastructure and business. It also helps plan local services for individuals, families and communities.

SBS broadcasts and publishes across more than 60 languages, using data from the Census to ensure its audio, digital, and television offerings reflect the country's evolving demographics.

The data is often used by researchers to study a range of topics, including population demographics, economic trends and social issues.

Do temporary visitor holders need to complete the Census?

International visitors, migrants, refugees and people on temporary visas (including international students and tourists) must also complete the Census.

People staying in hotels, motels, or bed and breakfasts can access paper Census forms from accommodation staff. Those staying in short-term rental accommodation (like an Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with internet access.

The Census is strictly confidential. Personal information such as names and addresses cannot be accessed by police, immigration agents or any government departments.

How can international visitors and students complete Census?

For international visitors and students staying in hotels, motels or student accommodation, instructions on how to complete the Census will be provided by accommodation staff.

Paper forms should be available at locations including bed and breakfasts, cruise ships, commercial vessels and snowfield accommodation.

More than 61,000 overseas visitors were counted in the 2021 Census amid the COVID-19 pandemic, compared to around 315,000 in 2016. Source: AP / Mark Baker

International visitors staying in holiday rental properties (such as Airbnb or Stayz) can complete the Census online with free internet access.

People staying in remote locations or free camping sites can visit Accredited Visitor Information Centres to access Census forms. The completed survey can be mailed via the provided Reply Paid envelope.

All details, including personal information collected during the Census, are strictly confidential and protected by law. The Census must be completed in English.

What help is available to complete the Census?

Online information about the Census is also available in 26 different languages via the ABS website. However, the questionnaire must be completed in English.

People who speak a language other than English can contact the Translating and Interpreting Service (TIS National) which provides access to interpreters who speak more than 150 languages.

The Census aims to capture everyone in Australia at a particular point in time, like a family photograph of the nation. Source: AAP

People staying in remote and regional Australia, including fly-in fly-out workers, are expected to complete the Census.

Around 30,000 ABS field staff have been employed to ensure all Australians, including people experiencing homelessness or in hospital, can access the form. In 2021, field staff travelled more than 10 million kilometres across Australia.

Field staff will also gather Census information from people in police custody on 11 August.

The ABS confirmed to SBS News that they receive administrative data for people in detention centres and correctional facilities within Australia, which provides necessary Census details.

What if you're travelling on Census night?

If a person is travelling within Australia on 11 August, they are still expected to complete the Census.

This includes anyone travelling overnight on a long-distance train, bus, or aircraft (including red-eye flights between Perth and the east coast), and on long-haul transport vehicles that are parked or in motion.

International visitors to Australia are expected to complete the Census. The form is available in hotel or motels and also online with access to the internet. Source: AAP / Joel Carrett

People must include information about where they are staying or whether they are in transit.

If an Australian is overseas on 11 August, they do not need to complete the Census.

If someone is completing the Census form at their usual address, the person travelling needs to be marked as 'away' but usually living at the dwelling.

Can you be fined for not completing the Census?

The Census is compulsory under the 1905 Census and Statistics Act.

If a person does not complete the Census when directed, they will receive a formal written direction to do so. If they refuse, they can be prosecuted and fined up to $364 a day.

What happens if you provide false information?

The Census asks up to 66 questions, including an individual's gender identity, ancestry and religious affiliation.

When asked about religion during the first-ever Census in 1911, 32 people identified as "Wowser" and 21 as "Angelic". In the 2011 Census, more than 64,000 people in Australia marked their religion as "Jedi".

Why is everyone counted in the Census?

The ABS maintains "every response matters" during the Census and helps determine the distribution of public funds. Providing false or misleading statements or information is considered an offence and can result in a fine of up to $3,640.

Liz Allen, a demographer at the Australian National University's Centre for Social Policy Research, said the Census is deliberately designed to provide a broad snapshot of the nation.

"It gives us an important reference point of who's in the country at that particular time," she told SBS News.

The Census is compulsory for all Australians, international visitors, temporary residents, migrants and refugees in the country. However, Australians who are overseas on 11 August do not complete the Census.

READ MORE What to watch out for as Census scammers go looking for victims

Generally, one person completes the form on behalf of their household.

Allen said that allows the ABS to collect information on "who might be staying over at a friend's house or gran's house" on Census night.

"So it's not just a Census of people. It's a Census of Population and Housing. It gives us essential information on ... how and where we live and then housing stock in the country."

The Census is usually completed online; however, individual and paper forms can be requested if preferred.

How to identify Census-related scams

As Census night fast approaches, Australians are being warned to look out for potential scams and report any inaccurate or suspicious information.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's Scamwatch told SBS News it had recently received reports of Census-related scams involving unknown parties "impersonating" the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS).

Field staff may drop off Census forms in person but are not allowed to enter your premises. Credit: ABS

"Scammers often take advantage of major events and trusted government services to make their contact seem legitimate," a Scamwatch spokesperson said.

"Australians should take a moment to stop and check before acting."

While the ABS said it's currently unaware of any scams related to the upcoming Census, the national statistics agency has said cold calls, fake text messages, and phishing emails are among the tactics scammers have used in the past.

The ABS is also reminding Australians that it will never ask for information such as:

Bank details or credit card information

Money or donations

Passwords

Identity documents or a tax file number.

It's also stressed that people will never be offered prizes or incentives for completing the Census, which is compulsory for everyone in Australia on Tuesday 11 August.

It will also never contact people via social media or ask for personal information without their consent. However, some Australians may also receive online communications if they register for updates through myGov.

title: The $28 billion plan at the centre of a growing FIFA storm
text:
In brief European football's governing body UEFA said it would boycott the World Cup if FIFA's privatisation proceeds.

Football Australia has asked for more time to consider the proposal.

Football's international governing body, FIFA, is facing a problem where some of its members have vowed to boycott all competitions if it creates a planned commercial subsidiary, valued at up to US$20 billion ($28.47 billion), that would sell a minority stake of up to 20 per cent to private investors.

On Wednesday, FIFA announced a proposal to create the entity, FIFA Forward Enterprise, which would be responsible for selling commercial rights such as broadcasting, sponsorship, ticketing, and licensing, as well as operating FIFA tournaments, including the men's and women's World Cups.

FIFA has promised each of its 211 member countries and territories US$40 million ($56.9 million) in funding for the 2027-2030 cycle if they agree to the plan.

However, the proposal received strong rejections from some of FIFA's six regional football bodies, with the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) launching a boycott of all FIFA's competitions.

In a strong statement on Friday, UEFA said FIFA's proposed model "has no place in world football".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Europe's position is clear. We will never lend this model our legitimacy. No one has the moral authority to sell what they merely hold in trust for the next generation," UEFA said.

The Confederation of North, Central American and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF), which represents 41 national teams in the Americas, also objected to the proposal but did not say whether it would boycott FIFA's competitions.

"History has shown FIFA and the football family what happens when the custodians of the game lose sight of these values," CONCACAF said.

Why did FIFA's proposal spark backlash?

According to FIFA, the entity was proposed after an address by FIFA president Gianni Infantino on the eve of this year's World Cup final in July.

During the address, Infantino said he intended to "unleash the commercial potential" of FIFA's competitions, including the World Cup.

"Football is the world's most popular sport and an extraordinary engine of human and social development," Infantino said.

"Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value — and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game."

Besides managing FIFA's commercial rights, the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise would allow private investors to make "minority, non-controlling investments" in the entity.

FIFA claimed the move was similar to other sports governing bodies that had "dedicated commercial subsidies", and stressed investors would be selected against "clear long-term, governance, and strategic criteria".

Infantino's funding promise to all 211 associations would include US$20 million ($28.44) as a one-off payment available from January for special projects, and the same amount in standard development funding over the course of the 2027-2030 cycle. Under the previous plans, member associations are set to receive around US$10 million in funding over that period.

However, the announcement was greeted by ire from bodies such as UEFA, which warned private investment in global football competitions would "change football forever".

UEFA also criticised FIFA for the short notice of the proposal, accusing it of "a profound failure of leadership" and "an abdication of FIFA's duty as the custodian of world football".

"It is both irresponsible and indefensible that a proposal of such significance for football was conceived in secret and brought to the brink of approval without any meaningful consultation with those entrusted with stewarding the game," UEFA said.

Australia's response

On Thursday, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), which Australia is a member of, also criticised FIFA's lack of consultation for its proposal.

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa called the move "totally unacceptable".

"The AFC notes with great concern and disappointment that it was not consulted by FIFA at any level prior to the public announcement of this proposal," Salman wrote in response to Infantino's letter.

"Furthermore, the AFC is deeply concerned that FIFA's unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency."

Salman also requested all member associations await the outcome of the consultations before taking any position regarding the proposal.

In a statement, Football Australia confirmed it has received correspondence from FIFA regarding the latest commercial proposal.

"As this is the first time we have been made aware of the initiative, we are now working to understand the proposal in full," it said.

"We have requested further information from FIFA to properly assess the strategic, commercial and governance implications of such a significant step."

Football Australia said it would only be able to form a position after receiving the information and engaging with peer member associations and the AFC.

Amid escalating rivalry between the United States and China, a pristine paradise in the western Pacific is confronting what it means to be part of the "tip of America's spear" in the region.

Home to around 18,000 people, the nation of Palau is comprised of hundreds of tiny, uninhabited, volcanic islands jutting out of the surrounding ocean. The archipelago is covered in lush vegetation and surrounded by turquoise lagoons and coral reefs.

The distinctive limestone islands that make the nation such an international drawcard are just a short walk from 18-year-old Dior Imaim Ngiraboi's home.

The recent high school graduate has fond memories growing up here, swimming in the crystal-clear water and playing in the nearby forest. Like so many Palauans, Ngiraboi has a deeply personal and cultural connection to the natural environment.

She meets SBS News at the water's edge on a typically warm morning. A few street dogs have risen from their slumber, watching with curiosity. It's here that Ngiraboi tells us about the traditional conservation concept of 'bul'.

"It's a very, very big part of Palauan culture," she says.

"It's something our ancestors knew was a necessity, to allow our environment to heal, to be able to continue providing for us. Growing up, we were told to take care of the environment because it's taking care of us."

Dior Imaim Ngiraboi is one of seven Palauan students who filed complaints with the United Nations challenging US military expansion in Palau. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

For Ngiraboi, that connection to the land is being reshaped by a changing strategic reality in the region.

Amid growing rivalry with China, the US has expanded its military footprint across these islands, and many Palauans are balancing hopes for greater security with concerns about the environmental, cultural and social costs.

In late 2024, Ngiraboi was among seven Palauan high school students who filed a complaint to two United Nations Special Rapporteurs. The complaint alleged the expansion of the US military presence in Palau was harming local communities and the natural environment.

The allegations have not been tested in court. The US says it takes concerns about its projects seriously but broadly disputes the students' claims.

Inside the US military expansion in Palau

The US has been steadily building and revamping military sites across Palau, including World War Two-era runways, naval facilities and sophisticated radar systems.

SBS News visited one of these sites, still under construction, which will eventually become an unmanned Tactical Mobile Over-the-Horizon Radar (TACMOR) transmitter.

According to its Environmental Impact Statement, the 22-hectare facility would "improve the United States' and its regional partners' ability to monitor air and maritime platforms in the vicinity of Palau and vastly beyond the horizon to enhance domain awareness, safety, and security".

The US military declined to provide further details about the site , citing the "sensitivity and special capability of the TACMOR".

The planned radar system in Palau will use over-the-horizon technology to monitor air and maritime activity across a wider area of the Pacific. Source: SBS News

However, the military showed SBS News its planned upgrade of Malakal Port, the main commercial hub serving Koror, Palau's biggest city.

The multi-million-dollar project would expand the port's length to approximately 250 metres, allowing large-scale vessels — including warships — as well as heavy equipment and personnel to move more quickly during times of crisis or regional contingencies.

Relations between Palau and the US are governed by the Compact of Free Association (COFA), a long-standing agreement under which Washington is responsible for Palau's defence and provides significant economic support in exchange for exclusive military access and strategic rights.

Sergeant Major Jimmy Castro, senior enlisted leader of the Joint Task Force - Micronesia, says the US force in Palau is "committed to building regional stability and security for the Pacific region".

"Our partnership with Palau serves as a warning to potential adversaries that any conflict in this region will be a grave miscalculation , " he tells SBS News.

Palau caught in US-China rivalry

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth has described the second island chain — a strategic arc stretching across the western Pacific that includes Palau — as the "tip of America's spear in the Pacific".

The second island chain lies in the middle of the western Pacific. It stretches from mainland Japan, passes through Japan's Bonin Islands, the US territories of the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam, extends to Palau and ends in Western New Guinea, Indonesia. Source: SBS News

In May, during a speech to the Shangri-La Dialogue — Asia's premier defence summit held in Singapore — Hegseth warned of "China's historic military buildup" in the region.

The following month, the Palauan government complained to the Chinese government about a Chinese-flagged research vessel that allegedly entered Palau's Exclusive Economic Zone without warning.

The complaint alleged that "the vessel appeared to conduct questionable research-related activities without authorisation, activities that threaten Palau's national security and disregard its sovereignty and rules-based order".

China did not publicly respond to the complaint, but has previously defended similar actions as compliant with international maritime law.

Jodean Remengesau, a Palau-based expert with the Pacific Center for Island Security, says: "It seems like they're testing the waters."

"It's not as aggressive, but they're making their presence known," she tells SBS News.

Jodean Remengesau says the US-China strategic contest will "impact us sooner or later". Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

Remengesau says the strategic competition between the US and China is shaping the security environment across the Pacific, including in Palau.

"We're in an oasis mindset. It seems like things these days are quite peaceful, but it'll impact us sooner or later," she says.

It's almost like the big elephant in the room that no-one wants to acknowledge.

Kambes Kesolei is a veteran Palau-based journalist and founder of the Compass Point Institute, the country's first locally established think tank.

Kambes Kesolei says the scale of US military activity in Palau is unlike anything he has seen since COFA came into effect in 1994. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

Kesolai says he's never seen this level of US military engagement since the COFA entered into force in 1994.

"Every time you put military installations in an area where there's high tension and geopolitical rivalry, you make yourself a target; you're in the crosshairs," Kesolei tells SBS News.

Palau's Taiwan dilemma

Palau is one of just three Pacific Island nations to recognise Taiwan as a sovereign nation.

Across the country, SBS News observed several development projects jointly funded by Taiwan, including the government's main administrative office and its capital building in Ngerulmud.

The Palaun Capitol building in Ngerulmd is among the infrastructure projects jointly funded with support from Taiwan. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

US Army veteran and Palauan resident, Tutii Chilton, says tensions between Beijing and Washington over Taiwan have left Palau "between a rock and a hard place".

"This is not our issue. Palau doesn't have any enemies. Our only enemies are our friends' enemies," he tells SBS News.

Despite having served in the military, Chilton says he now has serious concerns about his country's growing closeness to the US.

"I respect the military, I was a veteran, and I believe in it. And yet, people forget about the target that is put on your back."

US Army veteran and Palauan resident Tutii Chilton says rising geopolitical tensions are forcing Palau to confront difficult questions about its future. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

Chilton says the COFA means Palau has given the US significant responsibility over its defence and strategic affairs.

It's not democracy. It's profits, military expansion to hold on to profits, and businesses. That's the bottom line … it's still colonisation, 2026 style.

The US rejects the suggestion that the relationship is unequal, pointing to the compact's economic benefits, security arrangements and the voluntary service of many Palauans in the US military.

Asked whether he'd describe the relationship as "equal", Castro responds, "absolutely".

"The significance of the US-Palau partnership is definitely based on trust to maintain peace in the Pacific," he says.

The military also points out that Palauans serve in the US military at a higher rate per capita than any other nation, as well as most US states and territories, which it says "speaks volumes" about the relationship.

Former vice-president of Palau, Elias Camsek Chin, is another veteran with the US military. He served for 23 years across multiple continents and says the US presence in Palau has been a force for good.

Former vice-president of Palau, Elias Camsek Chin, says the US presence has helped maintain peace and security in the Pacific. Source: SBS News / Tys Occhiuzzi

"The US has been trying to maintain peace throughout the world for a long, long time , " the 77-year-old tells SBS News.

We don't have any enemies.

"It's the other countries that don't want to be friends with us."

'Deep concerns' from UN rapporteurs

Dior Imaim Ngiraboi and her fellow students submitted their complaint to the UN after interviewing residents across Palau through the community-based NGO Ebiil Society.

She says some residents described the lasting legacy of major World War Two battles, fought by US and Japanese forces on the southern island states of Peleliu and Angaur.

Unexploded ordnance from the conflict remains a safety issue in parts of Palau.

"When the military first came to Palau in World War Two, the damage was irreversible, and you can still see the effects to this day," she says.

"So, if that was then, what will happen now?"

In October, the students received a response from the group of UN-appointed Special Rapporteurs, expressing "deep concern" over reported breaches of Palau's environmental protection laws.

The UN Special Rapporteurs' response was based on the information provided in the complaint and did not constitute a legal finding against the US.

Castro says the military ensures compliance with local laws and environmental requirements.

"There are always concerns and inquiries regarding military construction projects, and we take that very seriously," he says.

But while military construction continues, Ngiraboi's activism goes on.

"I just hope they can take responsibility and proceed more with care, to be more considerate of the people and environment around them.

This is our life. They come to work. But this is our life, this is how we live. I want them to be able to respect it.

title: An issue of trust: The 'worrying' problem Australia faces
text:
IN BRIEF Australians' trust in each other has dropped to a low unseen this decade, with trust in democracy also declining.

Increasing political discourse about multiculturalism and national identity could be behind rising mistrust.

Australia celebrates the value of mateship, but distrust between the population has grown to the highest level reported this decade.

A survey of over 3,500 people, conducted by the Australian National University in June, suggests Australians trust each other less than they did during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Professor Nicholas Biddle, head of ANU's School of Politics and International Relations, said some of the findings were concerning.

"Worryingly, interpersonal trust among Australians has fallen to 5.32 on a scale of 0 to 10 — the lowest value recorded in ANUpoll during the 2020s,'' he said.

"This sits below the pre-COVID value of 5.53 recorded in October 2019 and reverses the increase in trust observed during the pandemic."
