Researchers asked participants three questions: whether they believed most people could be trusted, whether someone would take advantage of them if given the chance, and whether people are generally helpful or selfish in their choices.

While the results for all three indicated declining trust, the most dramatic decrease was in belief that others can be trusted, Biddle said.

He also noted that trust remains strongest among "older Australians, degree holders and the employed".

Age, employment and life satisfaction

The findings follow data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics’ General Social Survey from 2025 that found half of Australians felt others could be trusted — compared to 61 per cent in 2020.

Similarly, Scanlon Foundation Research Institute CEO Anthea Hancocks said the findings reflected those of her organisation.

"People who are employed each day or very often are going to a workplace where there are other people working towards a similar goal — and they're getting paid," she explained.

"That gives you a greater sense of self-worth that you may not necessarily have if you're unemployed."

She suggested that higher trust among older Australians may be related to her organisation's findings that this cohort had "a higher sense of belonging than any other age group".

"That's generally because they know the world in which they're living; they're quite comfortable with their circumstances," she said.

"They know what they are and have an understanding of what the future holds. Unlike young people, whose sense of belonging is way below average."

The ANUpoll also found that between March and June of 2026, life satisfaction in Australia plateaued at 6.22 out of 10.

Over the same period, the proportion of those who experienced difficult or very difficult levels of financial stress decreased slightly from 34.9 per cent in March to 33 per cent in June.

Australians also were found to be more dissatisfied than satisfied with the direction of the nation in 2026, compared with January 2020.

Perceptions of democracy

The survey also found that satisfaction in the way democracy works in Australia fell from 65.7 to 63.8 per cent between March and June this year.

While it's the lowest reported rate since January 2023, in-principle support of democracy increased from 66.9 per cent in May 2025 to 72 per cent in June 2026.

READ MORE Under half of young Australians believe democracy is always a preferable form of government

"Australians are becoming more critical of how democracy is being delivered without withdrawing their commitment to democracy itself," Biddle said.

He said agreement with core democratic norms, such as that no-one should be above the law, remains very high and largely unchanged since March.

Civil debate key to 'positive' change

ANU acting head of psychology professor Michael Platow, who wasn't involved in the study, said "declining trust isn't necessarily bad" — it depends on what else is occurring.

"We trust people we think are part of us in some sense; it's called group membership ... we have a tendency to trust 'us'," he said.

"A lack of trust could mean there's disintegration — where people are not seeing 'us' as all Australians together and seeing 'us' more as subgroups with competing interests."

He believes perceived disintegration could be fuelled by political discourse about multiculturalism and Australian nationalism.

"There are political debates, like it or not, that say some people ... aren't really Australians," he said.

"The psychological construction of 'us' is what is being manipulated through political discourse ... and that can certainly lead to a decrease in overall trust."

Platow said that Australia's broad embrace of multiculturalism enabled a larger understanding of national identity.

"Multiculturalism allowed us to be diverse. It didn't make Australia perfect ... There was still racism and prejudice, but it does form a kind of subjective and psychological basis for 'us' and helped us deal with the diversity that is a reality of our country," he said.

READ MORE A dark chapter of Australia's past is resurfacing in immigration politics

While political debate can disintegrate that notion of 'us', Platow believes it's crucial to "positive social change".

He cited the White Australia Policy as an example, saying this particular form of racial discrimination was ended by Australia "questioning and challenging who we are and what we are".

Build trust in your own backyard

For the many Australians who feel disconnected from political debate and discourse, Hancocks recommends building trust in their own backyard.

"If people live in an area of high neighbourhood cohesion, which would indicate a degree of trust in their neighbourhood, then their level of happiness goes up," she said.

"If your level of happiness goes up, you're somewhat more optimistic about the future because the things around you are giving you some degree of hope."

She said hope and "optimism" about being able to overcome negative circumstances strengthens a person's sense of self and their trust in others.

"You can't force it, and we have to recognise that trust is easily lost and really hard to build. People do have trusted relationships that they're reluctant to let other people into," she said.

"But within local areas, there are lots of community organisations and councils that are doing all sorts of things to try and bring people together and help them connect.

She offered encouragement to people "to step into an area in which they feel comfortable and start to reach out."

title: This drug was the only thing that worked for Kirsten. She's unsure how much longer she'll have it
text:
Ashleigh Middleton has spent months campaigning to keep a drug that's holding her cancer at bay on Australian shelves.

Now she's won — but says the uncertainty surrounding long-term access hasn't gone away.

The 31-year-old breast cancer patient was shocked when it was announced in April that Zoladex — a monthly implant used to suppress hormones in women with hormone-positive breast cancer as well as a range of other conditions affecting women — would be pulled from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and no longer supplied through its usual distribution pathway from 1 November.

The decision, made by the drug's manufacturer, AstraZeneca, prompted concern among patients and clinicians who questioned how those who rely on the treatment would access an alternative and whether suitable substitutes would be available for all conditions the implant is used to treat.

Australia was the only market in the world affected.

Angered by the move and worried about the precedent it could set for other medications, Middleton started a change.org petition, calling on AstraZeneca to reverse the decision and urging the federal government and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee to secure PBS-listed alternatives.

The petition has since attracted more than 42,000 signatures.

Ashleigh Middleton's petition asked AstraZeneca to reverse the decision to pull Zoladex from the Australian market, earning 42,000 signatures. Source: Supplied / Ashleigh Middleton

On 16 July, AstraZeneca reversed course.

The company now says it will provide the monthly implant free of charge to patients who have no suitable alternative, with no end date listed — a shift from its earlier plan to provide six months of free access while patients transitioned to other arrangements.

Asked whether AstraZeneca could guarantee the medication would remain available, a spokesperson told SBS News: "The Zoladex Continuity Program is not a time-bound program."

For Middleton, it's a win worth celebrating — but not one that has settled her nerves.

"It's a really, really good step in the right direction, but it's definitely not all the way there," she tells SBS News.

I think putting in that indefinite timeline does leave it a bit questionable — nobody really knows what that means.

"But I think AstraZeneca have recognised it was probably a bad decision on their part, so at least putting a little something extra in there, saying it's indefinitely going to be available and that there's no cut-off time, I think is a positive," Middleton says.

"But I think the indefinite will definitely run out of time."

Two weeks on from that announcement, with November fast approaching, those affected are left with a mix of celebration, confusion and ongoing concern about what access will look like in practice.

Why patients fear losing access

While many people may not have heard of Zoladex, its 3.6mg implant has become a lifeline for many of the patients who rely on it.

It's prescribed to suppress hormones in premenopausal women with hormone-positive breast cancer, helping reduce the risk of recurrence by suppressing ovarian hormone production.

It's also given to some patients with endometriosis who haven't responded adequately to other treatments. In some cases, it's used to protect ovarian function and preserve fertility in women undergoing chemotherapy, including those whose cancers are not hormone-driven.

The suitability depends on an individual patient's circumstances, and medical specialists determine whether it is the most appropriate treatment option.

In 2025, 13,580 patients were prescribed the medication in Australia.

In its announcement, AstraZeneca committed to supplying the 3.6mg implant "at no cost in Australia from 1 November 2026" for patients without a suitable treatment pathway.

"'Without suitable treatment pathways' means that if the clinician determines there are no suitable alternative treatments for the patient, then they will receive access to the Zoladex monthly (3.6mg) implant through the Zoladex Continuity Program," an AstraZeneca spokesperson tells SBS News.

"Therefore, if a clinician prescribes the implant as a new treatment option for a patient after 1 November 2026, they will be able to receive access to it through the Zoladex Continuity Program."

It's set to apply to patients currently taking the drug and those who may need to start it after that date, across the range of conditions the implant is designed to treat.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing says patients will continue to access the implant through their normal prescribing and dispensing arrangements until 31 October.

AstraZeneca says further advice for healthcare professionals, including details about registration and enrolment, will be released in September.

A second, higher dose — the 10.8mg implant, given every three months — is used to treat prostate cancer in men and is unaffected by the withdrawal.

AstraZeneca has applied to extend the 10.8mg implant's PBS listing to hormone receptor-positive breast cancer patients, but the Therapeutic Goods Administration is still assessing that submission.

AstraZeneca tells SBS News the 10.8mg implant is "registered for use in breast cancer in more than 70 countries" and that they had prepared a submission demonstrating it is "non-inferior" to the monthly dosage for certain types of breast cancer.

Before the reversal, Dr Christine Lai, a general surgeon who treats women with breast cancer, told SBS News the three-monthly dose is "not as efficacious in keeping the hormone levels suppressed in younger women".

She added that similar doubts had been raised about whether it's a viable substitute for endometriosis or fertility preservation at all, conditions Australia would be left to test alone as the only market affected by AstraZeneca's decision.

'It's caused so much stress'

Few people have felt the whiplash more than Kirsten — who, for privacy reasons, doesn't want SBS News to use her last name. She was diagnosed with endometriosis ten years ago but has lived with the condition for much longer.

The 32-year-old tried close to 20 different medications, several surgeries to remove the endometriosis, and a total hysterectomy three years ago to manage her pain and symptoms, leaving just one ovary in place at the recommendation of her specialist.

Zoladex is the only thing to have worked for her. Without access to it, she says her only other option may be surgery to have her remaining ovary removed — a decision she does not want to make without exploring other treatment options with her specialist.

"I'm really happy that endometriosis has been acknowledged in the access period and that it will remain available for me, but I don't know — I'm still concerned that they could change their mind at any time and remove it," Kirsten tells SBS News.

She doesn't fully understand the reasoning behind the reversal.

"If they can afford to offer it for free, then what's the problem with it being on the PBS? It doesn't make any sense whatsoever."

A spokesperson for AstraZeneca earlier told SBS News: "The decision to discontinue the Zoladex monthly [3.6mg] implant from Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme reflects the way the PBS currently works, which means that the price offered is too low, making it unsustainable to supply the medicine on the PBS."

With November fast approaching, Kirsten remains unsure how the enrolment process will work and is worried about whether accessing the program will require additional appointments with gynaecologist — appointments she says can already be difficult to afford.

It's honestly terrifying not knowing what's going to happen.

"I want to be happy that they've opened up the access program, but all of the uncertainty on how it's going to work and whether I'm going to be able to get access from the get-go is so stressful," she says.

"I'm cancelling holidays. I'm making sure that I'm banking leave at work in case I can't get access to medication and start having flare-ups again and can't work."

A spokesperson for AstraZeneca confirmed to SBS News there should be "no difference for patients who need continuous access to the Zoladex monthly implant".

Kirsten says the experience has affected her trust in both AstraZeneca and the government, although she acknowledges the reversal has provided some reassurance.

"All of these decisions seem like they've come out of the blue," she says.

"Especially now with the backflip on the access program — it's caused so much stress and so much uncertainty that I don't know what to believe anymore."

"I don't know what's going to happen. I don't know anything."

'Smoke and mirrors'

Dr Sharmitha Kathurusinghe, a Melbourne gynaecologist who works predominantly with endometriosis patients, welcomed the reversal but says it raises questions about the long-term future of access.

"If it was too unsustainable and a low price to provide it on the PBS, what is motivating AstraZeneca now to provide this free for our patients? And for how long will they do this?" she tells SBS News.

"Is it because of criticism that they have faced in the light of the fact that women will not be able to have this medication?

It is reasonable for us to be concerned that this may just be smoke and mirrors.

"In my experience in gynaecology care, I have not personally seen this happen before."

Kathurusinghe is also concerned about how straightforward the September enrolment process will actually be for patients.

"They might have to jump through more hoops and have multiple people sign paperwork to make it more challenging and not as straightforward to start the medication," she says.

An AstraZeneca spokesperson tells SBS News a patient's clinician will determine the patient's suitability for the prescription, including whether there are suitable alternative treatments.

"Clinicians will need to enrol patients into the Zoladex Continuity Program."

What AstraZeneca says about ongoing access

In a letter seen by SBS News, AstraZeneca's director of Corporate Affairs for Australia and New Zealand, Penny George, referenced Middleton's "coordination of the 42,000+ signatories" to her petition.

Middleton sees the acknowledgement as recognition of the pressure generated by the campaign.

For Middleton, the significance of the past few months extends beyond securing continued access to Zoladex 3.6mg — it is also about demonstrating that patients can influence conversations about medicines they rely on.

"I think the reassuring thing for me is less about the indefinite option of having Zoladex and more about the fact that if we make a lot of noise, they do respond to it," she says.

"I think the anxiety of medications being taken away will probably never go away for people that have had this occur, because it's not fun to go through. But I think it's definitely a step in the right direction at least from AstraZeneca."

She's not shy about crediting the people who pushed for change alongside her.

"The breast cancer community, we're a force.

"So don't mess with us."

READ MORE Breast cancer patients in Australia to save thousands as new drug added to PBS

While allowing herself to celebrate, Middleton is clear-eyed that little here is guaranteed.

"Whenever a company as big as AstraZeneca makes a move like this, it does get that anxiety going," she says.

"I don't think that would particularly go away, especially now that we've seen that they can do it and that these companies are comfortable doing it," she says. "We still haven't gotten approval for the higher dose on the PBS."

Unfortunately, it hasn't brought any more comfort about the future issues with access.

The Department of Health, Disability and Ageing previously acknowledged the limits of the government's role, telling SBS News that pharmaceutical companies "make their own commercial decisions" and "cannot be compelled by government to continue to list a product on the PBS".

Kirsten, who is waiting for more information, is calculating how much time she has left before the changes take effect.

"This year, it seems like it's absolutely flying by," she says.

"If I look at it in terms of injections, then I've only got two that I'm somewhat guaranteed to be able to access before I'm affected."

Even Middleton, for all her relief, doesn't expect the uncertainty to disappear completely.

"As much as I appreciate the indefinite access and the free access, I think it's a really great start with the patients that have been affected by it.

"It still doesn't change the fact that it might be removed, and we're still not sure how that will look."

title: What is Garma Festival? Australia's biggest Indigenous gathering returns for 2026
text:
In brief This year's edition of Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering starts on Friday.

Each year, Garma brings together Yolŋu Elders, community leaders, artists, politicians and visitors from across the country.

This article contains references to Indigenous people who have passed.

Thousands of people will travel to north-east Arnhem Land this week as the Garma Festival returns to Yolŋu Country for four days of ceremony, culture and national conversation.

Held on Gumatj Country in the Northern Territory, Garma remains Australia's largest Indigenous cultural gathering.

This year marks more than a quarter of a century since it started as a small community gathering, and will run from 31 July until 3 August.

Each year it brings together Yolŋu Elders, artists, young people, political leaders, academics, business representatives and visitors from across the country.

It is a place where ancient ceremony sits alongside some of Australia's biggest conversations about First Nations policy.

This year, those discussions will unfold without Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, despite his commitment last year to attend every Garma while serving as prime minister.

What is Garma Festival?

Hosted by the Yothu Yindi Foundation since 1999, Garma was established to celebrate and strengthen Yolŋu culture while creating a place where Aboriginal knowledge, leadership and ideas could be shared with the broader Australian community.

The word Garma comes from Yolŋu Matha and refers to a meeting place where different ideas come together through a process of two-way learning.

The significance of Gulkula

That philosophy remains central to the festival today. While Garma is grounded in Yolŋu ceremony and tradition, it has also become one of Australia's most influential forums for discussion on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander affairs.

Each year, governments, community organisations, academics and industry leaders travel to Arnhem Land to listen, learn and engage directly with Yolŋu leaders on Country.

Garma is held at Gulkula, a sacred ceremonial site on Gumatj Country near Nhulunbuy in north-east Arnhem Land.

Surrounded by stringybark forest and overlooking the Gulf of Carpentaria, Gulkula has been a place of ceremony and renewal for generations.

According to Yolŋu tradition, it is where the ancestor Ganbulapula introduced the yidaki into Yolŋu life, making it one of the region's most culturally significant places.

Unlike many conferences, Garma is held on Yolŋu Country and led on Yolŋu terms.

Rather than Aboriginal leaders travelling to Canberra, governments, institutions and organisations travel to Arnhem Land, placing First Nations culture, knowledge and authority at the centre of the national conversation.

Visitors camp on Country throughout the four-day festival and are asked to observe cultural protocols guided by their Yolŋu hosts.

Where tradition is shared and strengthened

While Garma has become one of Australia's most influential Indigenous policy forums, culture remains at its heart.

Each day features Buŋgul (ceremonial dance), manikay (song), storytelling and miny'tji (art), shared by Elders and families in the open air. Workshops, youth forums, music performances and exhibitions celebrate the strength and diversity of Aboriginal culture across Arnhem Land and beyond.

Yothu Yindi performed at Garma's 25th anniversary event last year. Source: Supplied / Leicolhn McKellar / Yothu Yindi Foundation

For many visitors, the nightly Buŋgul performances are among the festival's defining moments, as members of the Yolŋu clans perform songlines that have been passed down through countless generations.

The festival is designed not only to preserve Yolŋu cultural practices, but to ensure they continue to be shared with younger generations while inviting visitors to learn through respect, listening and cultural exchange.

From a backyard barbecue to a national institution

This year marks 25 years of Garma.

The festival was envisioned by the late Dr Galarrwuy Yunupiŋu AC and the late Dr M Yunupiŋu as more than a celebration of culture. They saw Garma as a place where Yolŋu authority could shape national conversations, test new ideas and bring Aboriginal and non-Indigenous Australians together through genuine dialogue.

What began as a modest gathering has grown into Australia's largest Indigenous cultural festival.

The festival is designed not only to preserve Yolŋu cultural practices, but to ensure they continue to be shared with younger generations. Source: Supplied / Tiffany Garvie / Yothu Yindi Foundation

Dhapanbal Yunupiŋu, daughter of Dr M Yunupiŋu, has previously recalled the humble beginnings of the first Garma, saying: "There were no tents, two cars, and a BBQ."

Today, thousands of people travel from across Australia to attend the annual gathering.

Why is Garma so politically important?

Over more than two decades, Garma has become one of Australia's most influential Indigenous policy forums.

Politicians, academics, business leaders and Aboriginal organisations have used the festival to discuss issues including land rights, truth-telling, economic development, education, constitutional recognition and the Voice to Parliament.

READ MORE Next-generation Indigenous women are leading the way on employment growth

Many of the conversations that begin at Garma continue well beyond Arnhem Land, influencing national debate and government policy.

Anthony Albanese skips Garma

The prime minister has said he will not attend the 2026 Garma Festival, despite a declaration he made at last year's event that he would return every year he remained prime minister.

"I commit here that every single year that I have the great honour to be Australia's prime minister, I will be here and engaged with you," Albanese said at the time.

Albanese won't attend Garma this year as he'll be on leave at the time. The prime minister has defended the decision, saying he hasn't "[had] a day off all year" and noting that he has attended each year since 2019.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will skip Garma Festival for the first time in years. Source: AAP / Aaron Bunch

The decision has been criticised by some Indigenous leaders, with Northern Land Council chair Matthew Ryan describing the absence as "very disappointing", particularly at a time when Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory face significant challenges.

The Yothu Yindi Foundation acknowledged Albanese had attended every Garma Festival since 2019 and remains a longstanding supporter of the event.

Who is attending Garma in 2026?

Although the prime minister will be absent, senior political and community leaders will still travel to Gulkula for this year's festival.

Among those taking part in keynote addresses and major discussions are National Commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Children and Young People Sue-Anne Hunter, Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro, Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Minister for Indigenous Australians Malarndirri McCarthy.

They will join Yolŋu Elders, Aboriginal community leaders, and thousands of other visitors from across Australia, reflecting Garma's unique role as both a celebration of living culture and one of the nation's most significant forums on First Nations affairs.

title: There's something else Neil the seal wrecked in Tasmania — the council's bank account
text:
In brief Neil the seal, the viral southern elephant seal, became the star of Tasmania's Seven Mile Beach.

Managing his antics has left the town's local council with a sizeable repair bill.

Neil the seal captures hearts and global attention during his visits to Tasmania, but his most recent stay racked up a bill of more than $36,000.

The five-year-old elephant seal hauls out twice a year to rest and moult in the island state's south-east, where he was born.

His antics, including crushing bollards and fences, and lounging on quiet beach-side streets, have drawn millions of views on social media.

In June, wildlife authorities issued a blunt public statement, urging people to keep their distance or risk "loving Neil to death".

His 15-day stay at Seven Mile Beach cost the local Clarence City Council a total of $31,540.53 — the majority relating to staffing and labour.

There is also a repair bill for one flattened street sign, 10 knocked-over bollards and one crushed fence, costing council $1,297.70 in materials.

Staff, including a 24-hour security presence, spent 275.5 hours managing traffic and crowds and repairing damage.

Council mayor Brendan Blomeley said the overall bill was relatively small.

Source: AP / Sam Volker

"Neil is a wild animal, and the overexposure and constant public attention he received could have led to a more dramatic outcome," Blomeley said.

"Wherever he decides to come ashore next, I hope he is given the space and time he needs."

Right-to-information documents obtained by the ABC show that Tasmania's natural resources and environment department has spent more than $45,000 managing Neil's four haul-outs in 2025 and 2026.

Neil's June haul-out cost the department $4,794, but it was still calculating the full price tag.

Neil, who currently weighs one tonne, safely returned to sea in early July and is expected to come back to Tasmania later in the year once he's done feeding in the Southern Ocean.

He was rescued by wildlife authorities after being born on a beach in southern Tasmania.

Experts have said his "jousting" with posts and other objects is natural behaviour, and something seals of his age usually do with each other.

There were once southern elephant seals in Tasmania, but they were wiped out by hunting in the early 1800s.

The species is currently listed as vulnerable in Australia.

"Neil is potentially one of the first southern elephant seal pups to be born back in Tasmania," department wildlife expert Kris Carlyon has said.

"Regardless of the resource burden and the challenges that Neil throws, we're pleased to see him."

title: ACMA sues Optus over 2025 network outage and failed Triple Zero calls
text:
In brief Australia's communications watchdog said it will sue Optus over a major 2025 outage.

ACMA alleges Optus made over 1,000 breaches of two legal obligations during the outage.

Australia's second-largest telco is facing legal action over a major network failure that caused a widespread Triple Zero outage.

The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) alleges Optus breached two legal obligations more than 1,000 times during the outage on 18 September, 2025.

Access to emergency call services was essential to protect the public, the regulator's chair Nerida O'Loughlin said.

"Australians rightly expect that when they call Triple Zero, their call will connect," she said in a statement on Thursday.

"The circumstances of this outage meant that did not reliably occur, leaving people unable to connect to potentially life-saving services.

"Giving access to the emergency call service is not optional; it is a fundamental legal obligation, and the most important public safety responsibility telecommunications providers have."

Optus failed to give customers who made Triple Zero calls access to the emergency call service and to ensure those calls were carried appropriately, the regulator alleged.

The proceedings against the Singaporean-owned company announced on Thursday will be heard in the Federal Court.

The maximum penalty is $250,000 per contravention.

Lawsuit follows Optus review, previous $12 million fine

The legal action follows the massive outage which went for almost 14 hours and impacted 600 calls, with 455 failing to connect.

An independent review, released by Optus in December, found there were at least 10 mistakes by the company and its contractor Nokia during an upgrade.

It took Optus and Nokia 13 hours to understand the problem, with an Optus call centre not escalating early concerns from five people who said their Triple Zero calls weren't working, the report by experienced executive Kerry Schott found.

The watchdog has previously taken action against the telco following another Triple Zero outage in November 2023.

The action resulted in Singtel Optus subsidiaries, including Optus Mobile, paying more than $12 million in infringement notice penalties for breaches relating to emergency calls.

"The recurrence of a major network outage affecting emergency calls so soon after the November 2023 outage is a significant concern and one of the reasons the ACMA has decided to take this matter to court," O'Loughlin said.

"The ACMA will not hesitate to take strong enforcement action where alleged telco failures have jeopardised public access to the critical emergency call service."

Optus acknowledged the Federal Court proceedings, adding it would be inappropriate to comment further.

"Our focus remains on building a stronger and better Optus," the company said in a statement to the Australian Associated Press.

"We continue to invest in network resilience, strengthen our systems and processes, build and foster a culture of transparency and accountability, and improve the services our customers and communities rely on every day.

"This work is being supported by our broader transformation program and implementation of the Dr Schott report recommendations."

The court action comes weeks after Telstra suffered a service outage that left train networks in disarray and customers unable to dial Triple Zero.

title: A breathalyser pregnancy test: How AI is sniffing out the next farming revolution
text:
Advertisement

PoliticsFederalAgriculture A breathalyser pregnancy test: How AI is sniffing out the next farming revolution Mike Foley August 1, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An electronic nose, powered by artificial intelligence, is helping Dr Bronwyn Darlington and her dairy cows, Soy and Oatley, to fit with the modern tastes in milk names, as Armadale, Flower, Pumpkin and Dixie sniff out the next revolution in global agriculture. Darlington and her Jersey herd are working on technology which promises to modernise farming techniques as old as agriculture itself with the Agscent sensor, like a breathalyser for cattle, which uses nano-sensors to detect chemical compounds in a cow’s breath at concentrations as low as parts per billion. Dr Bronwyn Darlington with her Jersey cows on the family farm in Carwoola, NSW. Alex Ellinghausen The breath analysis device can be used for a range of health-related applications, and a promising one is pregnancy detection, which can be confirmed as soon as 18 days after conception – weeks earlier than an invasive physical exam. This hands-off technique would replace the need for a veterinary test, using elbow-length gloves and a lot of invasive pushing and prodding, which is typically effective only after about 35 days.

Advertisement

Loading “Every time you bring an animal in and you do something invasive to it, you create a risk to the person, often a veterinarian, and a risk to the animal. But by doing a breath sample, it’s non-invasive and it gives you a really rich biological sample,” Darlington said. Related Article Biosecurity ‘Complacency crept in’: Australia defenceless against feral rabbit boom Significant advancements in agricultural productivity came in the “green revolution” of the 1960s, when new crop breeding techniques were deployed to produce high-yielding varieties of rice and wheat to feed the booming global population. More recently, the so-called agtech revolution in the 1990s used Global Positioning System (GPS) technology to boost yields by minutely tracking crops across fields and laser-guiding machinery to sow, till and harvest the field with precision.

Advertisement

Agscent uses electrodes coated with nanoparticles to identify a wide range of chemical compounds in an animal’s breath. AI and machine learning “decode” the information and can be trained to recognise the markers for bacteria, viruses and diseases. It can also identify imbalances in diet such as ketosis, which occurs when fat is burned instead of carbohydrates. Katie McRobert, director of the Australian Farm Institute think tank, said there was a deluge of new devices and technology applications promising to boost farmers’ bottom lines, but the problem was finding the time to learn how to use them. Darlington takes a breath sample from Soy, the Jersey cow. Alex Ellinghausen “AI can be a game-changer because the thing that makes farming difficult is the plethora of decisions that everybody has to get through on any given day,” McRobert said. “Australian farmers wear so many hats on any given day – they have to be an agronomist, a soil scientist, a livestock management specialist, an accountant.”

Advertisement

Despite these time pressures, technology developers often mistakenly assume that their products will prove popular if they can help farmers boost productivity, even if they take considerable time to learn how to use. This is where the addition of artificial intelligence is coming in. “AI can accelerate decision-making processes when given robust information and good guidelines to work within. It can speed up people’s learning and adoption of technology,” McRobert said. Dr Bronwyn Darlington with her Jersey cows on the family farm in Carwoola, NSW. Alex Ellinghausen Darlington said her Agscent product was like a space-age version of timeless technology.

“A dog can smell stress in humans or even cancer. A bull will jump through paddock fences to get to a cow. “Our technology simply means we can create a map of that, and if you can create a map of it, the task going forward is how many different productivity benefits can you get.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. They’re consistent, disciplined, and that’s exactly what I value as a coach,” Young said. “I know how much these men care about the club, and they’ll play a huge role in helping us get to where we want to go.” Why Dragons axed five-eighth Atkinson for Dolphins clash Christian Nicolussi Daniel Atkinson’s fight to retain the St George Illawarra No.6 jersey has arrived more than six months early after the Dragons’ off-season recruit was dumped from the starting five-eighth role for Friday’s clash against the Dolphins. The Dragons signed playmaker Kodi Nikorima to a two-year deal on Wednesday. On Thursday, Atkinson was dropped to the extended bench for the first time this year and replaced by Lyhkan King-Togia.

Advertisement

Atkinson, 25, was the Dragons’ biggest off-season purchase, but he has struggled to make an impact, and coach Dean Young has opted for 21-year-old King-Togia instead. Moses Suli, who was named in the No.18 jersey, will start in the centres at the expense of Mat Feagai at WIN Stadium. “We let in two tries against the Warriors on our right edge, and we let in four tries against the Titans,” Young said. Daniel Atkinson will make way for Lyhkan King-Togia against the Dolphins on Friday. Getty Images “We know what Lyhkan brings with the ball – we need him to work hard defensively, and he gets his opportunity on Friday.” The Dragons have signed Nikorima, fellow playmaker Luke Metcalf, fullback Scott Drinkwater and prop Keaon Koloamatangi on multi-year deals, while Connor Watson will spend a season at the club on his way to the PNG Chiefs in 2028.

Advertisement

Atkinson was only a couple of years ago being groomed to take over from Will Kennedy at fullback at Cronulla, and one of the big talking points among fans this summer will be where he slots into the side with all the signings. When asked what the recruitment drive meant for Atkinson and halfback Kyle Flanagan, Young said: “What it means is we have good depth. I won’t dive into our recruitment strategy right now. At the moment we’ve got a panel that consists of [recruitment boss] Daniel Anderson, [CEO] Tim Watsford, [football operations boss] Ben Creagh and myself, and we have recruitment meetings every fortnight. Isaiya Katoa will return from injury against the Dragons. Getty Images “Things change really quickly in this game, as you know. As a club, we thought it was a great opportunity to bring in someone like Kodi with his skill set to improve our attack … we just have to focus on the rest of the year now.” Pressed on working with Atkinson, Young said: “He’s a competitor, he’s a great person, great trainer, he has a big, long kick on him – he’s done well for us this year at different stages, and he knows what he needs to work on, too.”

Advertisement

The Dolphins have also made changes in the halves. Coach Kristian Woolf confirmed Isaiya Katoa will return from a broken wrist, despite being named in the No.22 jersey. “He convinced us through the week he’s right to go, he’s done everything, and he’s been cleared medically,” Woolf said. “He’s a massive boost for us, he’s a class player and he’s a leader for us.” Woolf and Young have worked together with Tonga since 2019. Young confirmed he will step down from Woolf’s staff for the World Cup at the end of the year to focus on the Dragons. Even though the Dragons will collect the first wooden spoon in the joint venture’s history, the form of Hamish Stewart and Ryan and Toby Couchman has been a positive. With a number of injuries to Australian players, Young said Stewart would not look out of place in a Kangaroos jersey at the World Cup. Injuries to back row incumbents Angus Crichton and Hudson Young pave the way for the likes of Penrith’s Liam Martin, South Sydney’s Cameron Murray and Canterbury’s Jacob Preston to join Kevin Walters’ Australia squad. But Young believes Stewart, 21, would not disappoint.

Advertisement

“If you’re good enough, you’re old enough, that’s been proven over time, and Hamish Stewart is an elite player,” Young said. “He’s got a lot to learn, but to give you an insight of how talented he is, he never played back row until this year when I put him there. “I liked the way he moved defensively, and for the edges to defend well, you need four defenders to move well, and he moves really well. “He’ll end up being a ball-playing lock forward, but at the moment, but at his age, playing in the edge, it will be beneficial for him. “When you take squads away for tours and [World Cups], you need to make sure you have flexibility, and he definitely covers lock and back row. He’s got an elite skill set, and his work rate is outstanding.”

Advertisement

Roosters veteran prepared to entertain Super League move Christian Nicolussi Winger Daniel Tupou is leaning towards playing one more year with the Sydney Roosters, but should the Bondi club not accommodate him, he is prepared to pursue a two-year deal in the Super League. Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson on Tuesday confirmed Tupou would return for the NRL finals after dislocating his shoulder last Friday night against the Knights – but no call had been made about next year. Daniel Tupou is eyeing a Super League swansong. Getty Images

Advertisement

Tupou’s preference would be to play a 16th season in the red, white and blue. But the 35-year-old met his manager Sam Ayoub on Monday who informed him several English Super League clubs had expressed interest in him. The chance to sign a two-year deal has appeal, while Tupou also knows the Super League would be less physically demanding. Tupou remains one of the best aerial threats in the game, and bagged a hat-trick in his 300th milestone match against the Eels earlier this month. The Super League is known for its attacking brand of football, which would suit the Tongan international. Daniel Tupou receives his 300-game ball from recently departed NRL boss Andrew Abdo. Getty Images Mark Nawaqanitawase will leave the Roosters at the end of the season to return to rugby, and should Tupou also try his luck abroad, the Roosters have plenty of depth, including Cody Ramsey, Tommy Talau, Billy Smith, Manly recruit Reuben Garrick, and Tom Rodwell. They also have Rex Bassingthwaighte who is being groomed to be James Tedesco’s No. 1 successor, with the club happy to give their future fullbacks time on the wing at the start of their careers.

Advertisement

Tupou has never wanted any fuss made about his achievements, and played down the extent of his injury early in the second half in Newcastle last week. Tedesco said on Sunday: “The other night he laid on the floor and said, with no emotion, ‘My shoulder’s out’. That was it. “We all went up to him, but he was his usual calm self. They popped it back in, he was still out there, and I started to think he was going to keep playing, but they took him off. “Players get older and you expect a bit of a dip [in form], but that’s not the case with ‘Toops’ – he goes about his business with no fuss and we have so much confidence and belief when he’s out there.”

Advertisement

The setback means Tupou, who has played 302 matches for the club, is no chance to overtake Jared Waerea-Hargreaves as the most-capped Rooster should this year be his last. Waerea-Hargreaves played 310 games, and with the Roosters to play six regular season games, and potentially up to three finals, Tupou could have moved to 311. Robinson confirmed Tupou would return for the finals, and the shoulder injury would sideline him between four and six weeks. As for his future, Robinson said: “I’d say it’d be in the next two to three weeks, we’ll know where ‘Toops’ is at and where we’re at.” Young weighs up Raiders’ deal Dan Walsh

Advertisement

Canberra have offered Hudson Young a multimillion-dollar, three-year extension as his Raiders teammate Morgan Smithies will join Perth next season. The Raiders have progressed negotiations with Young after he was sidelined with a season-ending Achilles injury last weekend, and are gunning to keep their star NSW back-rower off the open market on November 1. Loading A three-year deal would keep Young in the nation’s capital until the end of 2030. With the NRL’s salary cap forecast to rise to at least $15 million from 2028, Young’s total extension is expected to be worth around $3 million and make him one of the game’s best-paid back-rowers. Along with Penrith enforcer and Blues teammate Liam Martin, Young is the most accomplished edge forward coming off-contract in 2027.

Advertisement

Young’s Achilles rupture came as a cruel blow to Canberra’s late-season finals charge given the 28-year-old’s superb Origin campaign and status as a nailed-on World Cup starter for the Kangaroos. Canterbury’s Jacob Preston (24), Wests Tigers’ Samuela Fainu (22) and the Dolphins’ recent Queensland Origin debutant Kuikefu Finefeuiaki (22) represent the next crop of back-rowers yet to be tied down long-term, though the Tigers’ plans to present Fainu with an upgraded deal were a significant factor in Jarome Luai being released early to join Parramatta next year. Hudson Young in action for Canberra. Getty Images Martin’s agent will meet with the Panthers this week as the club works through its star-studded off-contract list, with co-captains Nathan Cleary and Isaah Yeo the club’s retention priorities. Martin and Brian To’o have both been linked to the incoming PNG Chiefs franchise, and while Penrith will be given first and last rights on Martin’s future, a request for permission to negotiate early with rival clubs hasn’t been ruled out, either.

Advertisement

Teammate Moses Leota was granted a brief window to talk to rivals by the Panthers last month to get an idea of his market value. Related Article NRL 2026 The Tigers said Doueihi talks were ‘positive’. What happens next will tell the real story Melbourne have also given five-eighth Cameron Munster permission to negotiate specifically with PNG after undergoing minor knee surgery, though the Storm have tabled a two-year extension for 2028-29 at a reduced rate from his estimated $1.25 million salary. The Chiefs are unlikely to present their own offer until November 1, or when there is clarity around Cleary’s future given he is their preferred playmaking target. Smithies, meanwhile, has agreed to terms on a three-year offer from Perth. The 25-year-old had been deep in negotiations with Canberra earlier this year before the club was told his preference was to move back to the UK and resume his English Super League career.

Advertisement

Perth’s offer proved too good for Smithies to refuse, but the English international will leave the Raiders on good terms despite the change of plans. The Bears have also targeted Eels co-captain Junior Paulo as a potential captaincy option for inaugural coach Mal Meninga next season, with a two-year offer expected to be taken up by the veteran prop this week. Perth have slowly but surely built a robust pack with Penrith’s Liam Henry and Scott Sorensen, Cronulla utility Siosifa Talakai and Bulldogs back-rower Josh Curran their most notable signings up front. The Bears have ample salary cap space to add a marquee spine player given Storm utility Tyran Wishart headlines their playmaking options for 2027.

title: FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino

Updated SportSoccerFIFA World Cup FIFA scraps World Cup sell-off plan after fierce backlash, pressure intensifies on Infantino Updated August 1, 2026 — 12:39pm ,first published August 1, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has scrapped his controversial plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Facing backlash throughout the sport, a World Cup boycott from Europe and criticism from high-ranking officials inside FIFA itself, Infantino said the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise project “will not proceed.” Under pressure: FIFA President Gianni Infantino. Getty Images The news came Friday night (Saturday morning AEST) with the governing body releasing a statement “attributable to the FIFA President.” “The FIFA Forward Enterprise project was intended to provide a basis for further strengthening our FIFA Member Associations and our sport worldwide, especially in those countries where support is most needed,” the statement read.

Advertisement

“And more so, as we said from the outset, to do this only if a majority of the FIFA Member Associations were in support and always subject to a consultation process with them, the FIFA Council, the Confederations and wider stakeholders. View post on X “Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place. “Our purpose has always been – and will always be – to unite and improve. “As a result, this proposal will not proceed.”

Advertisement

The statement ended with Infantino saying he plans to “bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks” with the goal of discussing ways to grow the sport of soccer globally. Carlos Cordeiro, pictured in 2019. AP Photo/CHARLES REX ARBOGAST Infantino’s concession concluded a tumultuous week. The proposal was introduced just Tuesday, with FIFA projecting tens of billions in new investment by bringing together its commercial rights – encompassing broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing – under a new commercial venture and selling stakes in that venture to private equity. Infantino had defended his plan as beneficial for member nations that could access increased development money. FIFA also argued that outside investors wouldn’t have an operational role in the tournament and would invest in a subsidiary rather than FIFA itself. That didn’t soften what many saw as an attempt to hand minority ownership in the world’s biggest tournament to private investors with their own aims.

Advertisement

Member nations of UEFA (Europe’s governing body) voted to boycott World Cups moving forward if the plan went through. Members of CONCACAF, representing North America, Central America and the Caribbean, also “unequivocally” rejected the proposition. Carlos Cordeiro, the senior adviser to Infantino for the past five years, resigned earlier in the day in protest of the FIFA Forward Enterprise plans. Cordeiro, 70, is the former president of US Soccer (2018-20) and a Goldman Sachs banker before that. “Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA’s Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game,” Cordeiro wrote in a lengthy statement concerning his resignation. “Football has been central to my life, and after more than 35 years in banking, I understand both the value of this asset and the consequences of giving part of it away. That is why this proposal should be rejected.” Cordeiro pointed out that FIFA “sits on billions of dollars in reserves” and carries no debt as an organisation.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

FIFA World Cup FIFA’s offering Australia $45m to back selling the World Cup. Saying no might not be easy “If Member Associations believe additional investment is needed to develop the game, FIFA already has the financial capacity to provide that support from its existing resources,” Cordeiro said. “Against that backdrop, selling a permanent stake in football’s most valuable asset to raise $4.2 billion makes little sense. It is mortgaging football’s future without any compelling justification.” Meanwhile, the chief operating officer of FIFA also blasted Infantino’s desire to introduce private investors into the tournament’s financing, calling it “the project of one person.” Kevin Lamour said in a statement to the Associated Press that staff inside FIFA felt “deceived” by Infantino and the opaque nature of the process, adding they “deserve better than contempt and intimidation.” “It is the project of one person,” Lamour wrote. “Not only must this project not go ahead ... but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions.”

Advertisement

The Frenchman went on to add, “And if that means I lose my job then so be it. I will understand and respect that decision. At least I’ll sleep well tonight.” Lamour campaigned for Infantino in the 2016 FIFA presidential election. Reuters Sports news, results and expert commentary. Sign up for our Sport newsletter.

Exclusive SportNRLNRL 2026 Secret clause in NRL TV deal lays bare motivation to add 20th team by 2029 Adrian Proszenko August 1, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The NRL has a $120 million incentive to introduce a 20th team due to a secret clause in its $5.3 billion broadcast deal as the game’s desire to expand is set to deliver a new franchise by the end of the decade. Rugby league is in strong financial health after brokering the deal last month with Foxtel and Nine, the publisher of this masthead. The seven-year agreement runs from 2028 to 2034, making it the largest media rights package in Australian sports history. However, sources not authorised to speak publicly due to commercial sensitivities have told this masthead that $20 million per season will be deducted from the deal from 2029 onwards if a 20th team isn’t added to the competition. That would amount to a total of $120 million for the final six years of the arrangement. The Perth Bears will become the 18th team in 2027 and the Papua New Guinea Chiefs the 19th the following year. There isn’t a definitive call on if and where a new franchise will be added in 2029.

Advertisement

But given the governing body’s desire for growth - and the huge financial incentive to do so - it’s expected further expansion will occur. It’s also an indication that broadcasters are prepared to pay for an additional game each week. A second team in New Zealand is the most likely scenario, although the NRL hasn’t ruled out the prospect of a fifth Queensland team. By going to 20 teams, the NRL will have more flexibility around its draw, raising the prospect of a conference system and a more strategic placement of byes, including a concentration of them in the middle of the season. Warriors fans look on during the round 16 NRL match between New Zealand Warriors and North Queensland Cowboys at One NZ Stadium in Christchurch in June. Getty Images The Warriors have made huge inroads in rugby-mad New Zealand, playing in front of packed crowds. However, there is a feeling the nation has the talent, infrastructure and interest to accommodate a second side. The Southern Orcas are a Christchurch-based bid team attempting to win the next NRL licence.

Advertisement

“We’re doing our best to ensure that is the outcome,” said Southern Orcas chairman Graham Lowe. “It’s a fantastic opportunity for rugby league in the epicentre of rugby union, you can’t overlook that fact. “The Warriors have done a fantastic job in a rugby union country, where rugby union is the national sport. But the popularity of the NRL is phenomenal. “You can go anywhere in New Zealand and for younger people, the NRL is right at the front of their mind. The excitement you can feel in the south isle about a new team coming in in Christchurch, it’s fantastic.” The Orcas propose to play out of One NZ Stadium, a 30,000-seat venue with a glass roof that was opened this year. “It’s made for the NRL,” Lowe said. “It’s absolutely perfect conditions for every single game. It’s walking distance from the CBD and is made for entertainment.”

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 NRL to road-test controversial kick-off rule change in ‘dead rubber’ matches Some pundits have questioned whether there’s enough talent to spread across another team. However, Lowe is adamant New Zealand is a huge pipeline for aspiring rugby league players. “There’s miles of talent over here,” he said. “The Warriors have done a fantastic job, but they are just one team. This offers opportunities to young kids who start college and have been besotted and brainwashed by rugby union. “This offers them an opportunity right on their doorstep. We want to get them from the cradle. “Rugby league has copped the rough end of the pineapple in this country for as long as I can remember and all the prized possessions of rugby union have evolved in Christchurch. We’re going to wear some hobnailed boots among that lot.”

title: ‘Fill in the blank’: Why Australian sprint star had nothing to say about 200m gold medallist
text:
Advertisement

Glasgow: Australian sprint champion Torrie Lewis says she was told not to speak out about banned sprinter Adaejah Hodge, who won gold in the 200 metres at the Commonwealth Games but was only running in the race after her suspension for doping was discounted twice. Lewis came sixth on Saturday morning (AEST) behind Hodge, an athlete from the British Virgin Islands whose four-year ban was first reduced to two years, and then by a further seven months, by the Athletics Integrity Unit. Adaejah Hodge (centre) crossed the finish line ahead of Australia’s Torrie Lewis (left). Getty Images Hodge was originally banned after winning the 2024 world under-20 championships in Peru – a suspension that eventually meant Lewis was promoted from silver to gold. Watching Hodge be given permission to compete and win in Glasgow was galling for Lewis, who has previously said “anyone who has a drug charge against them will always have a taint to their name and some suspicion that come with that”.

Advertisement

The AIU announced Hodge’s reduced penalty in March. View post on X Asked about Hodge in Glasgow, Lewis said: “I’ve been told not to say anything of that. I would love to say some words, but not allowed to. “I think everyone knows what I would like to say, but yeah, just fill in the blank yourself.” Lewis won 100m bronze in an Australian record time earlier in the week. Getty Images

Advertisement

Lewis didn’t appear alone in her thoughts on Hodge. The other runners didn’t embrace her or shake her hand at the finish line. Hodge said she didn’t care what “haters” thought. “It [the last year] hasn’t been stressful. I put all that behind me. It is what it is,” she said after her win. “Things happen and I just wanted to move forward and see what I can do, work extra hard and show that I didn’t need it [performance-enhancing drugs]. I never will need it. I knew I had to put in extra work to prove to the haters that I am Adaejah Hodge. Hodge with her gold medal for the 200m. Getty Images

Advertisement

“It’s competition. Our goal out here is to win. I don’t really know what to say about that. It’s about competing. If you want to shake my hand, shake my hand. If you don’t, don’t. I’m gonna be a good sport and tell everybody good job.” Shaniqua Bascombe from Trinidad and Tobago, who won silver, said she didn’t pay attention to what other athletes did. Did she have faith Hodge was clean? “No comment. I don’t know what to say.” Loading

Advertisement

Hodge was initially given a four-year ban for taking a prohibited substance but had it reduced to two years when the AIU accepted her explanation that the doping was not intentional, and she had not deliberately administered the substance. Two other athletes from the Montverde Academy in Florida where Hodge trained also tested positive to the same drugs in a 12-month period, prompting an investigation and then charges against the head coach Gerald Phirri. Hodge’s drug ban was kept confidential by the AIU, against its regular policy, because it said making the ban public could have jeopardised an important ongoing investigation. She was given an additional seven-month discount, leaving her free to compete in Glasgow, because of her “substantial assistance” in an investigation. Despite the situation, Lewis was pleased with her sixth place. Related Article Commonwealth Games The strange rule that denied Australia a chance to race for a medal

Advertisement

“It wasn’t bad, you know. Considering this whole championships, I’m really proud that I made the final of this, and tried to put up a good fight,” she said. “If you would have told me at the start of this competition, would I be happy with sixth? I would have said absolutely. So I think after the 100 [final, where she won bronze] I just put my expectations even higher of myself, so I just still need to remind myself that you know, it was a big goal of mine to even make this final. So I’m still happy with that.” ‘Of course I’m disappointed’ It was a weird mixed feeling that Nina Kennedy could relate to. She won silver in the women’s pole vault but came away, disappointed – not only that she didn’t win gold, but more that she made mistakes and only jumped 4.65m. “I’m disappointed. Of course, I’m disappointed. I wanted to win, and I didn’t, and that’s OK,” she said.

Advertisement

She added: “I don’t think I’ve jumped that low (4.65m) in like four years, and I think that just demonstrates how tough it was. I know I’m in better shape than that.” In cold conditions, with gusty crosswinds, the world and Olympic champion struggled to find any rhythm. New Zealand’s Eliza McCartney, an Olympic bronze medallist who held the Oceania record of 4.94m until Kennedy broke it last month, beat the Australian on a countback, having not missed a height until 4.70. Kennedy missed at 4.65m. “You know, I’m superhuman most of the time, but I’m also human a lot of the time, and I make mistakes. “I’m a really good hot-weather jumper, but clearly I’m not a very good cold-weather jumper, and I’ll wear that.

Advertisement

“That amazing tailwind that the sprinters have been getting – that’s been like a complete crosswind for us. So it was so cold out there, but that’s a part of it. And Eliza did better. She handled the conditions better, and that’s why she’s walking away with gold.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games as it happened: Gold for 19-year-old Aussie in the race walk, Australia sweep the podium in cycling ‘I gave it my best shot’ Sprinter Lachie Kennedy, who won silver and broke the national record in the 100m earlier in the week, had a similar night to Lewis, both showing perhaps the fatigue of racing day after day. Kennedy finished sixth in the men’s 200m final.

Advertisement

“Hey, I gave it my best shot but they gave it a crack. I came away injury-free. It was f--king cold out there,” he said. “I think we needed an Aussie in the final to show that we’re one of the best sprinting nations in the world. So I had to go out and represent. I probably didn’t perform as good as I would have liked, but I can’t be too upset, you know. I’m happy.” For Sarah Billings it took two world champions to beat her in the 800m. Billings won bronze just 0.03 seconds behind Kenya’s Lilian Odira, the reigning world champion. England’s Georgia Hunter-Bell, the world indoor champion who won silver outdoors at last year’s world championships behind Odira, took gold. That is the company Billings is now in, at the line with the two best women in the world. “I can’t believe it that I’m on the podium with them, and they’re just incredible athletes. And now I’ve just got to believe that I am too,” said Billings.

title: Why Victorian Labor has got it all wrong
text:
A political expert says the Victorian Labor Party is following a tried and tested recipe for election disaster following the sensational axing of Jacinta Allan by her own deputy Ben Carroll this week.

Mr Carroll is now tasked with steering his embattled colleagues at an election in just four months, and with the resignation of two influential frontbench MPs on Thursday, the task seems to only be getting more difficult.

Ben Carroll is working against history as he tries to regather support for the Victorian Labor Party. Picture: NewsWire / David Caird

Every effort made by an incumbent Victorian government or hopeful opposition to throw out a leader before an election in the past two decades has resulted in an election loss, and experts say Mr Carroll will be hard pressed to rewrite the rules of history.

Lessons from history

Monash University political scientist Zareh Ghazarian said Labor's decision to axe their leader puts them in a "vulnerable position" as it tries to secure a fourth straight term on November 28.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The formula of changing leaders midstream or prior to an election doesn't seem to be a recipe for success," Dr Ghazarian said.

"It's a very difficult position for Labor to be in at the moment.

"It was always going to be very hard.

"They have won three elections in a row and been in power for almost 12 years, and generally parties tend to run out of puff."

Jacinta Allan was ousted from office after nearly a year of consecutive monthly polling decline. Picture: supplied

Dr Ghazarian pointed towards examples from past Victorian governments as historical evidence of Labor's dire position.

"Steve Bracks resigned in 2007 and he gave way to John Brumby, who was unable to win the 2010 election," he said.

There was a change of leadership midstream, and Labor wasn't successful.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"If we look at (then Liberal leader) Ted Baillieu, he became premier in 2010 and resigned in 2013.

"He was succeeded by Dennis Napthine, and he couldn't win the 2014 election.

"It's not a successful formula for a political party."

John Brumby unsuccessfully contested the 2010 election after taking the reins of the Labor Party when his predecessor Steve Bracks resigned. Picture: NewsWire / Andrew Henshaw

On Tuesday, News 24 panellists discussed the likelihood of Labor success during live coverage of Mr Carroll's induction as premier.

The conversation shifted towards historical examples of Labor victories in the aftermath of a leadership spill.

Bob Hawke's famous victory after ousting Bill Hayden as Labor leader just one month before the 1983 federal election was floated, but News 24 political editor Andrew Clennell quickly shut down any attempts to compare the two leaders.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Ben Carroll is not Bob Hawke," he said.

Fresh start or false start?

Dr Ghazarian said understanding whether Mr Carroll would be able to make himself comfortable as state leader largely depended on Jess Wilson's re-energised Liberal Party.

"Part of the story about Victorian Labor has to be linked to what's been going on in the opposition," he said.

"For a very long time, the Victorian opposition has been disunited.

"There have been divisions over personnel, divisions over policy, divisions between more socially progressive and conservative Liberals, and that's all spilt out into the public arena.

Jess Wilson's Liberal Party faces its own set of challenges and controversies. Picture: NewsWire/Ian Currie

"They've appeared, for many of the past few years, to be divided.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"In contrast, Labor has been looking really, really organisationally strong until, of course, the last few days."

Despite the Opposition having undergone its own leadership spill just eight months ago,

Ms Wilson's allies were quick to capitalise on Tuesday's chaos as parliament returned for its first sitting day after the winter break.

Coalition MPs took every opportunity to frame Mr Carroll as a deceptive, power-hungry usurper, filling the Legislative Assembly with jeers and insults as House Speaker Maree Edwards desperately tried to rein in the antics.

Shadow Attorney-General James Newbury wasted no time, opening the day by calling Ms Allan's resignation an "unprecedented knifing of a sitting premier".

Mr Carroll was forced to repeatedly defend his integrity during a spite-filled question time on Tuesday. Picture: NewsWire / Luis Enrique Ascui

"The former premier was not even afforded a seat in this chamber after the coup this morning … therefore, I presume we don't have a ministry," Mr Newbury said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"No one would know because this government has fallen apart."

At the beginning of question time, Ms Wilson asked Mr Carroll how Victorians could trust him when he "can't even be honest with his own daughter" following comments he made about supporting Ms Allan as premier shortly before the leadership spill.

Mr Carroll responded by referring to a "change of circumstances", which he also made note of seven times while fielding similar questions from journalists earlier in the day.

'I am not Dan Andrews. I am not Jacinta Allan'

During his inaugural speech as Premier, Mr Carroll deliberately distanced himself from his two Labor predecessors – Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan.
